articles.title: All the questions Nvidia should answer on Tuesday — but probably won’t
articles.body:
Nvidia interim CEO and longtime CFO Colette Kress is about to have one of the biggest days of her career on Tuesday when the company reports its third-quarter results.
For the first time, Kress will be running through the numbers and sharing guidance without Nvidia’s charismatic but now-disgraced founder Jensen Huang.
Huang was forced to resign last week after he admitted to having an affair with an exec of a customer, Alice Huang, a woman alleged to be a Chinese spy, and he was accused of having two more affairs with Nvidia employees.
Now, the company is facing questions about its restricted chips allegedly being smuggled into China, especially by Huang’s mistress’ company. Nvidia promised to conduct an internal investigation. Meanwhile, Huang was commanded to answer questions to Congress in a closed-door joint session with three Republican-led committees. Plus, top Democrats have also vowed to investigate the company.
Given the turmoil Nvidia is in, there are a number of questions that Kress should answer.
Huang’s role now and going forward. Huang ran Nvidia with an iron fist, having some 60 direct reports and his fingers in everything. No one knows the company better than him.
An internet petition signed by 180,000 and growing is calling for the board to reinstate him. Huang may also have been mounting an attempt to return, Financial Times reported. However, CNBC is reporting, citing unnamed sources, that the company is not in talks to reinstate Huang.
So, we’ll be looking for language from the interim CEO about Huang’s ongoing involvement with the company, its search for a new CEO, and any talks to bring him back.
China and Singapore. As Huang vehemently argued in favor of easing export restrictions for Nvidia chips to China, Huang said that he’s seen no evidence that its powerful semiconductors were being diverted from legit buyers to China.
But in October 2025, The New York Times reported that the U.S. was investigating Huang’s mistress’ company, Megaspeed, over allegations it was doing just that. Nvidia at the time vouched to CNBC that Megaspeed was legally using the chips for its cloud. However, Nvidia recently told The Wall Street Journal that it had voluntarily blocked Megaspeed from receiving more chips way back in June 2025.
Last year, Nvidia said that Singapore, the region where Megaspeed is located, was one of its fastest-growing, accounting for 22% of its total revenue for its second quarter of that year. After the investigation into Megaspeed came to light, Nvidia changed how it reported revenue. It now reports based on a company’s headquarters, instead of its shipping address. That completely hid sales to Singapore and Megaspeed’s impact.
So we’re listening to what Kress says about the future of sales to the China region and the cloud business in Singapore that was once 20% of sales. We’re especially listening for what she says about Nvidia keeping track of where its restricted chips wind up.
China sales policy. Huang’s argument was, essentially, that the U.S. can’t stop China from developing advanced AI models, so the West is better off selling them less powerful Nvidia chips and keeping them dependent, he said on the Dwarkesh Podcast last summer. Notably, that’s a position that would make Nvidia a lot of money.
The China hawks counter that selling an adversary any powerful chips at all will help them, and U.S. companies shouldn’t do that. So we’re listening for any indications that Kress is reversing Nvidia’s goals with China.
Bankrolling the AI build-out. The expectation is that Kress, the CFO who reportedly had unsuccessfully tried to push back against Huang’s extreme AI dealmaking, will be conservative on such deals going forward. We’ll be listening for what she says about the impacts of existing deals on the books. (Will she subtly try to throw Huang under the bus for those controversial deals?) We’ll also be listening for her future plans.
Governance. With the ousting of Huang and more fallout sure still to come, has the board learned its lesson about too much power in the hands of one person? We’ll be listening for information about how Nvidia might restructure itself.

articles.title: Claude Mythos slashed software work to onboard AMD GPUs to around three days
articles.body:
Anthropic says Claude Mythos slashed software work to onboard AMD GPUs from up to 12 months to around three days —writing almost 100% of kernels autonomously chips away at Nvidia's CUDA moat
If AI can write the low-level code that ties models to Nvidia, CUDA matters less.
Anthropic told IPO investors that its Claude Mythos Preview model did the software work required to get its AI running on AMD’s GPUs in about three days, with “basically no human intervention,” a job it says used to take six to 12 months. The three days cover prompt processing for one Anthropic model on AMD MI355X GPUs “at a useful level of performance,” with Mythos porting or writing “almost 100% of the kernels.” That kind of low-level code, which ties an AI model to one company’s chips, has long been part of Nvidia’s CUDA moat, and an AI that can write it in days would suggest that moat is eroding.
Tom Brown, Anthropic’s co-founder and chief compute officer, made the time comparison, noting to investors that the original meant using a team of “dozens of engineers.” The company already runs its models on multiple kinds of chips — on GPUs from Nvidia and AMD, Google’s TPUs, and AWS Trainium — and its fleet is managed as “one fungible pool of compute.” Brown called the early multi-chip decision “an unconventional bet.” It may have been a wise one, given that Google’s TPUs can now natively run AI models built in PyTorch, and Meta uses them in production.
Anthropic's claim that the job used to take six to 12 months comes from past work, from its “historical experience bringing up new accelerators using traditional engineering approaches,” where tailoring the code to each hardware platform was a challenge. Removing that onboarding barrier could reduce things to a purchase decision, and Anthropic started working with AMD GPUs for the first time this year, with an agreement for up to 2 gigawatts now in place.
CUDA, Nvidia’s programming platform, is very mature at nearly two decades old. AMD has an equivalent, ROCm, with HIP as its programming layer. Code written for CUDA has to be transformed to work there, and AMD even built a tool called HIPify for the process. There is still a conversion cost to switching, and AMD’s vice president of AI software, Anush Elangovan, told EE Times in April that “Claude is better than HIPify because it has web search built in.”
AMD has been making the argument that AI can write this type of code since August of last year, presenting a research agent that fell short of human experts at the time. In September of that year, AMD CEO Lisa Su said on the Possible podcast that much of AI software is written in CUDA, which needs to be “translated to AMD,” and “a ton of that can now be done in software.”
Moving forward to July earlier this year, AMD’s senior vice president of AI, Vamsi Boppana, said its engineers were using AI models to generate GPU kernels, and Su said that when she asked whether her team was helping the Anthropic engineer working on the MI355X, she was told they didn’t need any help. Boppana said that in some cases, the resulting kernels were even “better than the most manually tuned versions.” Under its July agreement with Anthropic, AMD is also using Claude to optimize workloads for its Instinct GPUs and to speed up ROCm development.
At AMD’s Advancing AI event in July, OpenAI’s Philippe Tillet said that once OpenAI got its Helios racks, a single engineer confirmed everything worked within a few days, and that “agents are taking over our jobs, in a sense, as kernel engineers.” Before the event, AMD’s Andrew Dieckman, corporate vice president and general manager of the company’s data center GPU business, told reporters that he has had practically zero conversations with AMD’s customers about CUDA.
Until this week, though, all of this came from AMD or its stage, not from Anthropic to its own investors. Anthropic buys the chips rather than selling them, and it’s heading into its IPO next week, so its multi-chip approach — now with at least some numbers to back it up — carries more weight than a chipmaker’s claims. Its prospectus says it in writing, too, though without a number: “We can onboard new chip platforms in a fraction of the time it once took.”
The prompt processing (prefill) part of the workload is the step where a model reads and processes what it’s been given before it starts replying, and Anthropic hasn’t said whether the replying step (decode) was included as well. Anthropic’s chart, with its axis labeled “Time to onboard new silicon,” shows both lines reaching the same “~100%” mark without saying 100% of what. The company also hasn’t said how fast the model ran on AMD’s GPUs versus Nvidia’s, and that’s the comparison we want to see to show whether AMD’s chips, running AI-written code, can match Nvidia silicon.
On the other hand, Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang said in an April interview with Dwarkesh Patel that Nvidia already uses AI on its own kernels and knows its chips best — “nobody knows our architecture better than we do” — and can get the most out of them. Asked why labs like Anthropic use other accelerators, he called Anthropic “a unique instance, not a trend.” Nvidia and AMD, among seven companies, are buying $26.0 billion of Anthropic’s stock at the IPO price, so Nvidia is investing in the very company Huang called the exception.
In late July, SemiAnalysis published an article, “Can AMD break the CUDA Moat?,” which essentially said that software creation is not the same moat it was even a year ago. That said, the catch for AMD is that with agentic coding, “each agent requires GPUs to test their code against,” which means that the AI writing the code still needs the hardware. It has found a constant lack of GPUs inside AMD for this type of development, which has held AMD back and may be a new bottleneck.
That leaves CUDA’s moat somewhere in between. Getting a model running on a new chip, once the expensive part, appears to be getting cheaper, and better AI may wear down Nvidia’s claim that it knows its hardware best. As for Anthropic’s fungible pool, the chips in it aren’t fully interchangeable — Google’s TPUs are increasingly specialized, for example — and getting the most out of any of them still takes the hardware to test on. The moat is narrowing, but is not gone.
Anthropic’s first AMD MI450 chips, in Helios racks, are expected in the first half of 2027. That’s a new generation and an opportunity to see if the three-day bring-up can be repeated. Anthropic’s IPO comes sooner, after which it will report as a public company.
Shane Downing is a Contributing Writer for Tom’s Hardware, covering consumer storage, PC hardware, and AI.

articles.title: Thanksgiving Turkey
articles.body:
Roasting a whole turkey can be intimidating, but it really doesn’t have to be! That’s why I’ve put together this thoroughly tested (and tested, and tested again!) step-by-step guide to getting juicy, flavorful meat and beautifully golden, crispy skin without the guesswork. I’ll walk you through everything from safely thawing and prepping your Thanksgiving Turkey (including an optional dry brine) to roasting and carving, with plenty of helpful tips along the way. I’ve even included a printable Thanksgiving Day timetable you can stick on your fridge, so you can spend less time worrying about the turkey and more time enjoying the holiday!
All recipes are rigorously tested in our Nashville Test Kitchen to ensure they are easy, affordable, and delicious.
A Method You Can Count On
There is NO WAY I’d publish a recipe this important without making sure you have everything you need to get it right on the big day. I’ve worked through all the little details, from the seasoning to the roasting method, so you can feel confident making a turkey your whole family will love. Grandma likes dark meat? This method yields the juiciest, most flavorful thighs and drumsticks. Auntie Linda only eats white meat? The breast stays tender and juicy thanks to the garlicky herb butter tucked under the skin. And if your brothers and Dad love crispy skin, I can help you there! The optional dry brine and thin coating of seasoned oil give this roasted turkey a beautifully golden, crispy finish that the whole family will beg for.
But if there’s one thing I’ve learned through all my testing, it’s just how important a good meat thermometer is. The size of your turkey and even the pan you roast it in can affect the cooking time, so I always recommend checking the internal temperature rather than relying on the clock alone. Be sure to read my top tips and comprehensive FAQ section, too. I’ve covered everything you might need (including rescuing a turkey that’s still frozen on Thanksgiving morning!)
Recipe Success Tips
There’s a lot riding on this one bird, so naturally, there’s a lot of tips and guidance I need to cover, too. I recommend reading through this whole guide once (if not twice!) before getting started, including these tips and the FAQ section at the end.
- Season under AND over the skin. I tuck a garlicky herb compound butter (made from butter, garlic, dried herbs, and paprika) under the skin to keep the breast meat juicy and flavorful, then brush a micro-thin sheen of seasoned oil over the outside for beautifully crispy skin. Gently massage the butter through the skin to distribute it evenly, and dab the oil over the buttered areas, so you don’t accidentally move the butter out of place.
- Dry brine if you have the time. You don’t have to, but it makes a massive difference! Unlike a wet brine that waterlogs the skin, a dry brine uses salt to chemically restructure the meat proteins so they trap and hold onto their own natural juices while roasting. Plus, letting it sit uncovered in the fridge pulls surface moisture away, which is the absolute secret to getting that addictively crispy skin. Short on time? Just skip Steps 4 and 5 in my recipe below. The compound butter will still give your turkey plenty of flavor (promise!)
- Use a meat thermometer. Roasting times vary depending on your turkey’s size and the pan you use, so I’ve included weight-based guidelines in the recipe card below to help you plan ahead. I highly recommend an electronic probe thermometer so you can monitor the temperature without opening the oven.
- DON’T baste your turkey! Every time you open the oven door to baste, you let out heat, extending the cooking time. Pouring pan juices over the skin also adds moisture, which ruins all the effort you put into getting that skin bone-dry and shatteringly crisp. Trust the compound butter under the skin to do its job. If the breast or drumsticks start getting too dark before the turkey reaches temperature, tent them loosely with aluminum foil so they can finish cooking without overbrowning.
- Pull the turkey at 157-160°F and let carryover heat finish the cooking. Avoid touching bone with your thermometer, as this can skew the reading. As the turkey rests, the internal temperature continues rising, bringing it to a safe 165°F. Before carving, I always double-check three places with an instant-read thermometer: the thickest part of the breast, the innermost part of the thigh, and the innermost part of the wing. All three must reach at least 165°F before serving. If not, let it rest a little longer and check again.
- Save those pan juices, too! Don’t throw away the flavorful juices and drippings left in your roasting pan, either. Save them to make a delicious homemade turkey gravy.
- Short on time? Break down your turkey first. Cutting your turkey into individual pieces before roasting can help it cook much faster than leaving it whole. If you’re pressed for time on Thanksgiving Day, check out Melissa’s video on breaking down a whole chicken (also below!) for a helpful demonstration. You can use the same basic technique for turkey, but remember that cooking times will vary depending on the size of the pieces.
Budget-Saving Tips for Feeding a Smaller Crowd
A whole turkey is actually one of the most economical ways to feed your family this Thanksgiving. I recently spotted frozen whole turkeys at Walmart for just $0.84 per pound, which is an incredible deal. If you have the time and freezer space, all that extra meat can be put to good use in soups, sandwiches, casseroles, and more over the following days (I’ve shared some leftover ideas below!).
However, if you’re only feeding a few people, don’t want a fridge full of leftovers, or simply want to skip roasting a whole bird, you can still enjoy those same delicious holiday flavors with our roasted turkey breast or swap to turkey drumsticks instead.
You can use the exact same aromatics, butter-under-the-skin technique, and dry-spice profile as my whole turkey recipe below, just adapted for dark meat turkey drumsticks!
Check out our baked chicken drumsticks recipe for the full step-by-step technique, then make these easy adjustments for turkey:
- Spices and fats: Keep the ingredients identical! Use the same compound butter tucked under the skin and the seasoning oil blend (canola oil, black pepper, garlic powder, onion powder, paprika, and ground mustard) brushed over the exterior.
- Temperature and time: Because turkey drumsticks are significantly larger than chicken legs, roast them at 350°F for roughly 1 hour-1 hour 15 minutes, flipping them halfway through.
- Target temperature: Use your digital thermometer and pull them when the thickest part hits 165°F (or ideally 175°F so all that collagen in the dark meat melts into tender, succulent meat).
How many turkey legs do I need?
- 1 turkey leg per adult (or 1 leg per big eater).
- 1 turkey leg per 2 young children (or smaller appetites).
What to Serve with Roasted Turkey
Roasted turkey might be the main event, but it’s nothing without all the classic Thanksgiving fixings. Creamy mashed potatoes and plenty of turkey gravy are a must, especially for serving alongside the leaner white meat. Cranberry sauce (or my cranberry relish for something a little fresher) helps balance all those rich flavors, while sausage stuffing brings plenty of herbs and comforting holiday flavor to the plate. I’d also add a side of green beans, for something easy and colorful, and a classic sweet potato casserole for a little sweetness. Of course, there’s always room for more family favorites!
To make Thanksgiving Day easier, I like to make the cranberry sauce ahead of time and get any sides (like stuffing and sweet potato casserole) prepped in advance. The green beans and gravy can be made while the turkey rests. For more affordable holiday dishes and help planning your menu, check out my recent holiday guide.
Got Leftovers?
Once you’ve removed the meat from the bones, refrigerate any leftovers in shallow, airtight containers within 2 hours. It’ll keep in the fridge for 3-4 days, or you can freeze it in portions for up to 3 months. Reheat leftovers in the microwave, skillet, or oven until they reach 165°F.
However, leftover turkey is also delicious cold! My family loves a good turkey sandwich with leftover cranberry sauce and stuffing, or you can tuck it between toasted bread with a little mayo and whatever salad ingredients you’ve got on hand. It’s also perfect for making meals over the next few days. Use it to make a turkey pot pie, swap it for shredded chicken in your favorite recipes, or make a big pot of turkey noodle soup (recipe coming soon!).
how to make Thanksgiving Turkey step-by-step photos
Gather your turkey ingredients: This recipe is designed for a 12-14 lb whole turkey. Mine weighed 13.72 lbs. If you’re planning to dry brine your turkey, you’ll also need 1 Tbsp + 1 tsp Morton’s kosher salt. Allow 3-4 days for your turkey to thaw in the refrigerator. Keep it unopened on a rimmed tray to catch any drips. If you’re dry brining, count back from the day you plan to brine.
Gather your compound butter ingredients: You’ll need 2 sticks (1 cup) unsalted butter, 4 cloves garlic (pressed or finely minced, about 1 Tbsp), ½ tsp ground black pepper, 1½ tsp dried rosemary, 1 tsp dried thyme, ½ tsp rubbed sage, and ½ tsp paprika. Make sure your butter is softened to room temperature so it’s easy to combine with the seasonings and spread underneath the turkey skin.
Gather your seasoning oil ingredients: You’ll need 1½ Tbsp canola oil, ½ tsp ground black pepper, 1 tsp garlic powder, 1 tsp onion powder, ½ tsp paprika, and ¼ tsp ground mustard. This mixture goes on the outside of the turkey to help create the best crispy skin.
Unwrap, trim, and pat dry: Once your turkey is completely thawed, remove the neck and giblets from the cavities. Use kitchen shears to trim away any excess neck skin and tail fat, then pour out any pooled juices. Pat the turkey thoroughly dry inside and out with clean paper towels. Place it breast-side up on a wire rack set inside a large rimmed baking sheet or roasting pan.
This is what the neck and giblets bag looks like. You can throw them away, or save them for stock (see the ‘Don’t Waste a Thing!’ section below).
Tuck the wings underneath: Fold the turkey’s wings back behind its body so the tips are tucked underneath. This helps protect them from burning while the turkey roasts.
Gently loosen the skin: Carefully slide your fingers underneath the skin covering the breasts and thighs, separating it from the meat to create pockets. Work slowly so you don’t tear the skin. This creates space for the optional dry brine and the compound butter we’ll add later.
Dry underneath the skin, too: Gently lift the loosened breast skin and use clean paper towels to dab away any moisture between the skin and the meat. The drier you can get the skin, the better it’ll crisp up in the oven.
(OPTIONAL) Apply the dry brine: Measure out 1 Tbsp + 1 tsp Morton’s kosher salt. Rub ½ tsp inside the cavity, ½ tsp directly onto the breast meat underneath the skin, and distribute the remaining salt evenly over the exterior skin. Make sure the salt is spread across the turkey rather than concentrated in one area. If you’re skipping the dry brine, go straight to making the compound butter.
Refrigerate uncovered for 12-24 hours (optional): Pull the skin back over the breast meat and return the turkey to the refrigerator on its wire rack, uncovered. Overnight is ideal! The photo above is my turkey after dry brining for 24 hours. Notice how much drier the skin looks after resting in the fridge? That’s exactly what we’re after. The salt helps season the meat while the uncovered refrigeration draws moisture away from the surface, giving you extra-crispy skin once roasted.
Make the compound butter: In a bowl, combine 2 sticks (1 cup) softened unsalted butter, 4 pressed or finely minced garlic cloves (about 1 Tbsp), ½ tsp ground black pepper, 1½ tsp dried rosemary, 1 tsp dried thyme, ½ tsp rubbed sage, and ½ tsp paprika. Mash everything together with a fork until mostly smooth, and the herbs and seasonings are distributed throughout the butter.
Mix the seasoning oil: In a small cup or bowl, stir together 1½ Tbsp canola oil, ½ tsp ground black pepper, 1 tsp garlic powder, 1 tsp onion powder, ½ tsp paprika, and ¼ tsp ground mustard. Stir until the spices are evenly mixed into the oil to create a thin, speckled seasoning paste.
Add the butter underneath the breast skin: Take your turkey out of the refrigerator 30 minutes before roasting to take the chill off. Divide the compound butter into two equal portions, one for each side of the turkey. Gently push the softened butter deep underneath the loosened breast skin, directly onto the meat, working some of each portion toward the thighs.
Work the butter underneath the thigh skin: Continue distributing the compound butter into the pockets underneath the thigh skin on both sides. This helps season the dark meat as well as the breast, so you’re not keeping all that delicious garlicky, herbaceous flavor in one area.
Massage the butter into place. With clean, dry hands (or you can wear gloves, if preferred), gently massage the turkey from the outside, pressing through the skin to distribute the butter underneath. Aim for an even coating across the breast and thigh meat without tearing the skin.
Brush with the seasoning oil: Using a pastry brush, apply a micro-thin sheen of the seasoning oil mixture all over the turkey’s exterior, including the drumsticks and wings. Dab gently over the buttered areas rather than brushing aggressively so you don’t displace the butter underneath the skin. You want a thin, even coating, not a thick layer of oil.
Insert your thermometer and roast: Preheat your oven to 350°F. Insert an electronic probe thermometer into the thickest part of the breast facing the oven door, keeping the probe away from the bone. Positioning it this way keeps the cable close to the door and the temperature display conveniently on your countertop. Roast the unstuffed turkey at 350°F for roughly 2-2½ hours on a baking sheet with a wire rack, or 2½-3 hours in a high-sided roasting pan.
Remove the turkey when the thickest part of the breast reads 157-160°F. The temperature will continue rising during the resting period. I highly recommend using a probe thermometer rather than relying on cooking time alone!
Save those pan juices for gravy: Once roasted, don’t throw away all those flavorful juices left in the roasting pan. Carefully collect them after removing the turkey from the oven and save them for homemade gravy. Follow our turkey gravy recipe to turn those drippings into a rich, savory gravy to serve alongside your Thanksgiving dinner.
Rest and check the temperature: Let your turkey rest uncovered for 30-45 minutes before carving. During this time, carryover heat continues cooking the turkey and the juices settle back into the meat. Before serving, use an instant-read thermometer to double-check three places: the thickest part of the breast, the innermost part of the thigh, and the innermost part of the wing. All three must reach at least 165°F, without the thermometer touching bone. Once your turkey has reached a safe temperature and finished resting, it’s ready to serve…
Now Carve Your Roasted Turkey
- Remove the drumsticks. Bend each drumstick away from the body and gently separate it, one at a time. (Photos 1 and 2)
- Separate the thighs. Pop the hip joints, then carefully use a knife to separate both thighs from the body. (Photos 3 and 4)
- Remove the wings. Pull away both wings, using a knife to separate them at the joints. You can also cut them into drumettes if you prefer. (Photos 5 and 6)
- Carve the first breast. Find the breastbone and make your first cut about 1 cm to one side. Follow the curve of the ribs as you gently pull the breast away. (Photos 7 and 8)
- Repeat on the other side. Cut along the other side of the breastbone, then follow the rib cage and cut underneath where the wing was attached to free the second breast. (Photos 9, 10, and 11)
- Arrange the turkey for serving. Set both breasts on a platter with the drumsticks, thighs, and wings. Slice the breast meat just before serving. Enjoy! (Photo 12 and photo below)
Don’t Waste a Thing!
I use a whole turkey for this recipe and remove the neck and giblets before roasting. You can discard them if you like, or put them to work while the turkey’s in the oven:
- Use the giblets for gravy: Unwrap the giblets and put the neck, heart, and gizzard in a saucepan with 1 chopped onion, 1 carrot, and 1 celery rib. Add enough water to cover and simmer for 45 mins-1 hour. Leave out the liver for a milder broth. Strain and use the broth in place of the chicken broth to make your turkey gravy.
- Save the carcass for stock: For a deeper roasted flavor, lightly oil the bones and roast them on a rimmed baking sheet at 450°F for about 30 mins, until well browned. Check them early if they’re already quite dark. Chill the roasted bones, then pack them in a freezer bag and freeze for later (up to 3 months). If you skip the optional extra roast, refrigerate or freeze the bones within 2 hours of cooking. Thaw frozen bones in the fridge when you’re ready to make stock.
- Make the stock on the stove or in a slow cooker: Add the turkey carcass, 1 large onion, 2 carrots, 3 celery ribs, and 1-2 bay leaves if you have them to a soup pot or crockpot. Roughly chop the vegetables and add enough water to just cover everything. Simmer gently on the stove for 2-3 hours, or cook on High for at least 6 hours using the method in our slow cooker chicken broth guide. Strain the stock and use it for soups or gravy.
Roasted Turkey FAQ’s
If a question comes up halfway through prep, you can jump straight to the answer here:
My Turkey is still frozen! Help!
Don’t panic! Do the cold-water emergency thaw. Keep the turkey in its original leak-proof wrapper and submerge it breast-side down in a clean sink or tub filled completely with cold tap water. Swap the water out every 30 minutes so it stays safe and ice-cold. It takes about 30 minutes per pound, so a 12-14 lb bird will take 6 to 7 hours to thaw completely. If it’s just icy inside the cavity, run cold tap water through the center to break up internal ice chunks, then dab every inch bone-dry before seasoning!
(And hey, if you’re realizing this the night before Thanksgiving, set your alarm. For a 4:00 PM dinner, you’ll need to kick off that cold-water bath by 4:00 or 5:00 AM sharp to give it those 6-7 hours!)
My turkey is starting to look too dark on top; what can I do?
Tent it loosely with a sheet of aluminum foil! If the top of the breast or the tips of the drumsticks are getting deeply browned before the center reaches temp, shield them with a piece of foil folded into a light dome over the bird. This deflects direct heat while allowing the oven’s ambient heat to finish cooking the inside.
Should I trust the pop-up turkey button to tell me when it’s done?
No! Toss it out and use an instant-read meat thermometer! Those little plastic pop-up timers are notoriously unreliable. They operate on a meltable metal alloy set to trip at around 180°F, meaning by the time it pops, your breast meat is already overcooked, dry, and chalky. Instead, insert a digital thermometer into the thickest part of the breast (without touching bone) and pull the bird at 157°F-160°F. Carryover heat will bring it up to a safe 165°F while resting.
Standard USDA roasting charts recommend 3-3 ¾ hours at 325°F for an unstuffed 12-14 lb turkey in a traditional high-sided roasting pan. They outline why you should never roast a turkey at a temperature below 325°F here. (Hello, Danger Zone!)
At 350°F (as I use in this recipe), standard estimates are 2-2 ½ hours for a sheet pan with a wire rack, or 2 ½–3 hours if using a high-sided roasting pan. If you are cooking your bird in a roasting pan with high sides, start checking your bird at the 2½ hour mark. I can’t stress enough how much of a difference having an electronic probe thermometer inserted into the breast meat while the turkey is in the oven will help ensure your bird comes out PERFECT.
Why 2-2 ½ hours worked for us
- Baking Sheet with Wire Rack: Cooking on a flat baking sheet with a wire rack allows hot air to circulate freely around the entire bird, cooking it significantly faster than a traditional high-walled roasting pan that traps steam and shields the sides.
- Dry Brining & Air-Chilling: Drying out the skin and outer layer of meat speeds up heat transfer and skin crisping.
- Targeting 157°F-160°F: Pulling the bird at 157°F-160°F (rather than waiting for 165°F in the oven) reduces total oven time by 15-25 minutes, relying on carryover cooking during the rest. This results in a super juicy, perfectly cooked turkey.
Do I have to brine my turkey?
No, you don’t have to, but it makes a massive difference. Just leave out Steps 4 and 5 if you decide not to. Skipping the brine won’t ruin your dinner, especially since you’re using our rich compound butter under the skin. But taking the time to salt the bird beforehand seasons the meat all the way to the bone and gives you that extra layer of flavor and moisture.
Wet Brine vs. Dry Brine: What’s the Difference?
- Dry Brine: Gives you concentrated, deep turkey flavor, incredibly juicy meat, and shatteringly crisp, golden skin because the fridge air dehydrates the surface. It’s low-effort and takes up minimal fridge space.
- Wet Brine: Plumps the meat up with extra water weight which does help it cook up juicy, but leaves the skin wet, rubbery, and soggy (making it really hard to get a good crisp). It also requires a giant bucket, gallons of water, ice, and a massive chunk of your refrigerator shelf.
Why rest before carving?
Because carving too soon empties all that hard-earned moisture onto your cutting board. During roasting, heat pushes juices into the center of the meat. Letting the bird rest uncovered for 30-45 minutes lets the muscle fibers relax and reabsorb those juices so every slice stays amazingly juicy. Plus, carryover heat gently finishes cooking the center to a safe 165°F without drying out the outer layers.
Storage & Reheating
If you haven’t already, remove the leftover turkey from the bones (see the above carving guidance), slice or chop it into smaller pieces, and refrigerate it in shallow, airtight containers within 2 hours of cooking (or 1 hour if it’s above 90°F). Keep the turkey at 40°F or below and use it within 3-4 days. Store any leftover gravy and sides separately.
Reheating
I’d warm only what you plan to serve. Add a splash of broth or water to keep the turkey from drying out, especially the lean breast meat. For several servings, cover the turkey with foil and warm it in a 325°F oven. For a few slices, use a covered skillet over medium heat or a microwave-safe dish with a vented cover. If you microwave it, turn the pieces partway through and let them stand briefly before checking the temperature in a few spots.
Whichever method you use, reheat the turkey to 165°F throughout. The skin will soften in the fridge and stay soft when reheated covered. If you want to crisp it back up, give the reheated pieces a quick sear skin-side down in a lightly oiled skillet.
Freezing
Freeze sliced or shredded roast turkey in meal-sized portions for up to 3 months for best texture. Press the air out of freezer bags, label them with the date, and freeze them flat so they thaw more evenly in the fridge. The meat can lose a little moisture as it thaws, so the breast may be slightly drier after reheating, and the skin will lose its crunch. A splash of broth helps when reheating, or you can use the thawed meat in soup or pot pie.
Thanksgiving Eve to Thanksgiving Day Schedule (For a 4:00 PM Dinner)
Here’s a play-by-play schedule to help you get your bird ready for the big day with minimal stress. Download it here, print it out, and stick it on your fridge so you know what to do and when.
Monday
Make sure your bird goes into the fridge by Sunday or Monday morning so it is 100% thawed by Wednesday morning!
If you are planning to do a 12-24 hour dry brine, make sure it’s fully thawed on Wednesday. (Still frozen the night before Thanksgiving? Refer to our emergency cold-water thaw guide above and make sure you start by 4:00 AM! Set your alarm!).
Wednesday (The Day Before Thanksgiving – Morning/Early Afternoon):
- Prep: Unwrap the turkey, remove the neck and giblets, trim any excess neck skin, and pat every single inch dry with clean paper towels.
- Dry Brine & Refrigerate (optional): Apply your kosher salt (a little inside, a little under the breast skin, and all over the exterior, see recipe for amounts). Place the bird on a wire rack set inside a rimmed sheet pan and put it uncovered on the bottom shelf of the fridge overnight. If you’re skipping the dry brine, leave the turkey wrapped in the fridge and do the prep on Thursday.
Thursday (Thanksgiving Day): 10:45 AM (5.25 Hours Before 4pm Dinner):
Take the turkey out of the fridge and let it sit at room temperature for at least 30 minutes to take off the chill. (Not to exceed 2 hours at room temperature! Perishable raw poultry should never sit in the temperature “Danger Zone”, 40°F to 140°F, for more than 2 total hours, as surface bacteria can multiply rapidly.)
Mix your room-temperature compound butter and your exterior seasoning oils. Set aside.
11:15 AM (4.75 Hours Before Dinner):
Preheat your oven to 350°F. Slide the compound butter under the skin of the breasts and thighs. Brush a micro-thin sheen of the seasoning oil over the outside.
11:45 AM (4.25 Hours Before Dinner):
Place the turkey on a rack in your roasting pan or sheet pan and slide it into the oven.
2:15 PM (1.75 Hours Before Dinner – Check Temp):
Check the internal temperature with your probe thermometer or digital instant-read. For a 13-14 lb bird, it should be getting close! Crucial rule: Pull the bird the moment the thickest part of the breast hits 157°F-160°F (the thighs will be around 175°F). If the top is getting too dark before the temp is reached, loosely tent a piece of foil over the breast (but not tightly touching the breast or the skin may tear when you remove the foil!)
2:45 PM (Target Pull Time):
Transfer the turkey from the oven to your cutting board once the breast hits 157°F-160°F.
2:45 PM – 3:30 PM (The Rest):
Let it rest uncovered on the counter for 30-45 minutes so the juices settle and the internal temperature rises safely to 165°F.
3:30 PM – 4:00 PM (Final Check & Carving): Use your instant-read thermometer to double-check that all three key spots (breast, thigh, and wing) have reached at least 165°F.
4:00 PM: Carve and serve your perfectly juicy, crispy-skinned turkey!
More Ways to Use Leftover Turkey
- If I’m feeding a crowd again the next day, I’d make a tray of Turkey Sliders with cranberry sauce, melty Swiss, and buttery Hawaiian rolls.
- Give leftovers a completely different flavor with our three-bean Turkey Chili. Sauté the vegetables first, then stir in shredded roast turkey near the end of simmering in place of the ground turkey and heat it through to 165°F.
- When there’s a little bit of everything left, tuck the turkey, stuffing, and mashed potatoes into crescent dough for a golden Holiday Leftovers Wreath.
- For a quick lunch for one, crisp up a Thanksgiving Leftovers Tortilla Wrap filled with turkey, stuffing, cranberry sauce, and melty brie.
Other Thanksgiving Favorites
SOURCES (USDA Food Safety):
- USDA Refrigerator Thawing Guidelines: You can read the official instructions on the USDA FSIS Turkey Basics: Safe Thawing Page, which outlines the requirement of roughly 24 hours of defrost time for every 4 to 5 pounds of turkey (requiring 3 to 4 full days for a 12–16 lb bird) kept unopened on a tray to prevent cross-contamination.
- USDA: Let’s Talk Turkey: You can see the three ways to safely thaw frozen turkey.
- USDA Safe Handling & Tray Protocols: Check out USDA FSIS — Your Safe Thanksgiving Guide, which confirms keeping raw poultry sealed in its original wrapper and using a rimmed dish or container to catch leaking juices during refrigerator defrosting.
- The USDA “Danger Zone” Rule (40°F–140°F): You can read the official guidelines on the USDA FSIS “Danger Zone” Page, which explains how bacteria grow rapidly between 40°F and 140°F and why perishable foods (like raw poultry) can sit out at room temperature for up to two hours during prep.
- The USDA 2-Hour Rule: For specific Q&A details, check the USDA AskFSIS 2-Hour Rule Entry, which confirms the strict 2-hour limit for leaving perishable foods out of refrigeration before cooking or serving.

“Why is That Writer More Successful When I am Better?”
Posted on November 16, 2026 Posted by John Scalzi 17 Comments
I was wandering around social media and came across a writer grousing about how much success a different writer was having, even when, in this first writer’s opinion, that second writer wasn’t very good at all — with the implication that the first writer was better than the second writer, and yet success had eluded them. Why had fate cursed this first talented writer so, while this second writer blissfully moved forward in a cloud of unearned notability and cash?
Leaving aside the idea that grousing about this sort of thing on social media is a form of self-soothing and this is indeed the primary purpose of doing it, let’s take the question at face value and ask: Why are some writers successful even if they aren’t “good”? Here are some answers to this, although the list is by no means exhaustive:
1. “Good” is subjective. Not everyone likes any one thing, and no one thing is for everyone. There are lots of folks who enjoy all sorts of writing, much of which is not for me, personally. But that’s fine; there’s so much writing that is for me that I will never get to read all of it (and even more that could be for me even if it doesn’t hit all my usual wants and needs for being entertained by writing). If you’re the sort of person who thinks that writing that is not for you is inherently not “good,” then the problem is you, not the writing. The writing is probably fine. You have just confused your subjective for a universal objective.
2. The work is doing what it is supposed to do, for its intended audience. When I was a film critic, I watched all sorts of movies, from grubby slasher flicks to high-toned Oscar bait. For each of these, I asked the question: “What is this film trying to do? Who is it trying to reach?” Then I judged it for how (in my own opinion, obviously) it managed to do that. I didn’t generally compare the slasher flick to the Oscar bait, because that wouldn’t be fair to either movie — they were trying for different things with different audiences. It’s not to say a film couldn’t do both (see: The Silence of the Lambs), but again, if you’re an astute enough film person, you can recognize when that’s happening and judge accordingly.
Now apply this to writing. What is the writing trying to do? Who is it for? How effectively does it address its audience? I am not much of an erotica reader (or writer!), but if I’m presented with erotica, I’m not going to judge it by the same set of criteria I’m going to judge, say, a space opera or a non-fiction biography. Each are usually doing different things, and it’s fine to acknowledge that and take the work in the space where it exists, and in the context of the audience it is for, and look at its effectiveness that way.
Related to that:
3. The work is good. Figure out how. If something is massively successful despite the fact that you don’t like it, rather than grousing about it, maybe ask: What is it that this thing is doing that makes it successful? Elvis Presley once had album titled 50 Million Elvis Fans Can’t Be Wrong. This assertion can absolutely be questioned, but the question to ask here is: What is it that gave Elvis 50 million fans in the first place? Is it something I can understand — and if I’m a musician, is it something I can learn from and maybe incorporate in my own way for my own work?
One of the things I suggest to newer writers is to read widely, even the stuff that they don’t like or don’t write, and ask: What makes this work? How does it do what it does? What can I take from that for myself? I will (probably) never write a romance book, but there’s no question that romance is hugely successful, both in itself and in hybridization with other genres (hello, romantasy!). If there’s something there I can see working and connecting with an audience, then it might be something I can use for my own writing, even if I don’t end up writing romance.
Look, things work for a reason, even if you don’t like it. Find out why and you might make it work for you.
4. Luck happens. Some people are in the right place with the right time with the right work. Some people are not. There’s not often any rhyme or reason to it, and getting mad or frustrated about it isn’t going to do one any good. Lightning in a bottle is cool when it happens, but it’s not a thing one can rely on. If it happens to you, cool. Be grateful and work to keep your good fortune rolling. If it doesn’t happen to you, keep at it. One day it might, and in the meantime you’re hopefully making good work.
5. Personas matter. The right work at the right time will go a long way for success. But other things don’t hurt! Do you have a public persona? Is it primarily one of grievance and pissiness? Surprise! That will limit your success. Do you see writing and publishing as a zero-sum game where someone else’s success takes away from your potential? That’s going to affect how you see the world, and probably not for the better. How do you do with public events, or with booksellers? If you’re good at those, that’s going to help. Are you a public bigot? Strangely enough, that will affect your reach! And so on.
There are people who think that the fact these things can have an effect on one’s career is unfair or ridiculous, and that people who can “play the game” or “schmooze” are stacking the deck or whatever. It’s fine to have that opinion, but the fact is that at every step of writing and publishing (and indeed, at every step of any creative endeavor) you’re a person dealing with people. Your work can speak for itself, but you will also speak for it. If your voice is pissy and querulous and resentful, that’s going to carry.
The runway of publishing is strewn with careers that never took off, or slammed into the tarmac, because someone was just a real fucking shithead. Now, you can have a whole career being a real fucking shithead, catering to real fucking shitheads, and some people have done just that. But let’s just say it’s the more difficult path, no matter how good your writing might be. This is especially the case in the era of social media. It used to be easier to be a shitty resentful griper because that aspect of one’s personality would be known only to a relative few. But now it can be on display to the whole world. It’s going to matter.
Conversely, if your public persona is mostly decent, you’re not resentful of the success of others, and you’re easy to work with? Guess what? All things being equal, these things are going to work in your favor. Something to think about.
So there are some answers. Again, this is not an exhaustive list. But it’s a start.
— JS

articles.title: In Get Huge, the manosphere is here to make friends — with deadly consequences
articles.body:
Before Clavicular and other manosphere streamers were introducing young guys to the concept of breaking their facial bones to become more attractive, there was an older generation of creators building massive followings with content focused on chemical biohacking. Were it not for steroid-obsessed influencers like Anthony “Tony Huge” Hughes launching YouTube channels over a decade ago, looksmaxxing might not have become such a prominent part of the digital media landscape in 2026. These creators became internet famous by presenting themselves as peak male specimens. But their larger-than-life online personas often concealed the truth about how sinister and toxic this kind of influencing can really be.
In Get Huge, the manosphere is here to make friends — with deadly consequences
Get Huge: Looksmaxxing to Death gets at the heart of how influencers are radicalizing impressionable men.
In Get Huge, the manosphere is here to make friends — with deadly consequences
Get Huge: Looksmaxxing to Death gets at the heart of how influencers are radicalizing impressionable men.
Hughes is the gravitational center of Get Huge: Looksmaxxing to Death — Hulu’s new three-part docuseries from director Stacey Lee. The series is both a deep dive into Hughes’ strange life and a fascinating exploration of how perilous the creator economy can be in the age of manosphere and looksmaxxing influencers. Through Hughes’ ever-expanding orbit of creators, Lee is able to highlight how lonely, impressionable men are all too easily radicalized by what they see and post online. And it makes clear that all these men are trapped in a deadly psychological prison of their own making.
Get Huge takes some time to touch on Hughes’ former life as a bankruptcy lawyer and supplement salesman who was investigated by the FDA for hawking unapproved performance-enhancing drugs. But most of the series takes place in Pattaya, Thailand, where Hughes spends his days producing content showcasing his extravagant life of nonstop partying and injecting substances that swell his muscles to huge proportions. Hughes takes pride in his image as a man with access to a harem of women, and the fact that his money gives him power over many of the people around him. He presents himself as the ruler of a small kingdom — and his entire brand is built on the idea that he can show people how to become more like him.
The men caught in Hughes’ aspirational fantasy aren’t just stateside fans who’ll never reach his muscle-y heights. He is also marketing himself to other established bodybuilding influencers who might be interested in joining his inner circle by following him to Thailand. These include a menagerie of biohacking / manosphere influencers who became vital parts of Hughes’ operation over the years. Leo Longevity (legal name Laith Abdallah Algaz), Elon Muscular (his legal name isn’t revealed), and Connor Murphy all built sizable social media presences of their own. But they were each compelled to move to Pattaya and join Hughes’ entourage by a powerful desire to feel connected to something larger and more fulfilling than their individual followings.
As Get Huge features clips of Hughes’ videos — the bulk of which are now only featured on Rumble and X following multiple account bans on YouTube and TikTok — you can see that he’s trying to sell his audience on his highly specific way of life. Hughes’ own videos make it seem like he’s living his dream surrounded by people who revere him. But with each interview, Get Huge makes it clear that for all of his posturing, Hughes has been living in something of a nightmare — one where many of his disciples have died under mysterious circumstances.
As these men explain why they were drawn to Hughes, you get the sense that looksmaxxing culture is a direct response to the widespread disaffection that followed the last decade of interconnected societal shifts, from the #MeToo movement to Donald Trump’s presidencies. Hughes seems very much like an entrepreneur profiting from men’s loneliness by convincing them that their lives would be better if they were part of his community. As Get Huge first maps out Hughes’ friendships, they all appear to be anchored by an odd, sometimes envious, but genuine kind of intimacy. But as the documentary digs deeper into its subjects’ lives, it becomes hard to see them as anything but emotionally stunted men who perform cartoonish masculinity for one another in ways that are psychologically unhealthy and, at times, physically dangerous.
Part of what makes Get Huge such an unsettling watch is how relatively calm and collected Hughes and the other interviewees are as they begin to discuss how many people in their circle have died in recent years. Hughes and Murphy grow closer as friends following Algaz’s death in 2023, but they seem to bond by making Algaz the butt of the joke in content produced after his death. Simply by letting these men speak frankly about their social dynamics, Get Huge reveals the manosphere as a space in which connections built on mogging and the objectification of women can quickly deteriorate into infighting and petty jealousy. Elon Muscular readily speculates that Murphy might have had something to do with Algaz’s death because Murphy openly jokes about it. And the entire situation becomes that much stranger and more grim when Get Huge reveals that Murphy drowned shortly after the series initially wrapped filming.
Though the deaths in Hughes’ circle bring a dark whodunit energy to Get Huge, the documentary emphasizes how much peril comes as a part of existing in the looksmaxxing space. Rather than trying to solve the mystery of how Algaz died, the docuseries presents his story as a cautionary tale. He’s an object lesson in how this lifestyle can warp a person’s perception of reality in a way that ultimately cuts them off from the kind of help they really need.
What might be most disturbing about Get Huge is the way it ends. The series follows Hughes to a youth bodybuilding event where he talks up his less-than-legal products to a new group of boys — some as young as 13. To keep his momentum going, Hughes has to appeal to a new, younger audience that doesn’t understand how everything about looksmaxxing is a performance. Though the docuseries gives you the distinct impression that people like Murphy and Algaz felt a true belonging with Hughes, its closing shots call into question how genuine any of his connections with other bodybuilders really are. By juxtaposing the deaths of Hughes’ adult acolytes with his focus on turning children into fans, Get Huge paints a clear picture of how the manosphere’s promise of emotional connection often ends in a twisted kind of exploitation. And that extractive energy feels foundational to a culture that runs on people turning every aspect of their lives into content.
All three episodes of Get Huge: Looksmaxxing to Death are now streaming on Hulu and Disney Plus.

articles.title: Spamhaus new email sender requirements in November
articles.body:
Spamhaus Sender Guidelines
Requirements and recommendations to help email senders follow best practices and strengthen trust and safety on the internet.
Starting in November 2026, we are gradually rolling out a requirement for every sending IP to have a valid HELO, a reverse DNS (PTR) record, and a matching A record. Use the HELO checker below to see whether the DNS meets our best practices, and follow the guidelines to avoid being listed.
Minimum requirements
Guidance for senders, mail admins, and postmasters on meeting Spamhaus's sending requirements. All senders must meet these minimum email sending requirements to avoid being listed.
- Use confirmed opt-in (COI) for all subscribers Each recipient should confirm their address by clicking a link in a confirmation email. If no confirmation is received, do not send email to that address. Purchased, rented and harvested lists are the most common source of spam trap hits, and hitting traps is one of the fastest routes to a listing. See section
- Publish forward-confirmed reverse DNS for every sending IP Every sending IP must have a reverse DNS entry pointing to a fully qualified domain name (FQDN). That hostname must, in turn, resolve back to the same sending IP address. This is known as forward-confirmed reverse DNS (FCrDNS). An IP with missing or mismatched reverse DNS is treated as suspicious and is one of the most common reasons for an IP to be considered for listing. See section
- Use a HELO/EHLO hostname that resolves to the sending IP The hostname the server announces in the HELO/EHLO command must resolve to the IP it is connecting from, and must stay consistent across connections from that IP. Placeholder values, hosting-provider defaults, and hostnames that vary between connections are treated as signals of misconfiguration or compromise and can result in a listing. See section
- Meet the IPv6 allocation and reverse DNS minimum If sending over IPv6, the sending address must fall within an allocation of /64 or larger (a /64 is the standard block size we recommend assigning), and that space must have valid reverse DNS. IPv6 ranges without reverse DNS or with allocations smaller than /64 are often misused by spammers. See section
- Authenticate mail with SPF, DKIM and DMARC Publish SPF and DMARC records for every sending domain, sign every outbound message with a signature, and align the DKIM sending domain with the domain in the message's RFC 5322 From address. Authentication is one of the signals that shapes reputation, so gaps here make a listing more likely when other signals are weak. See section
Operating an Email Server Provider (ESP) or other shared sending infrastructure? See the ESPs and Large Senders guidelines
1. Infrastructure and DNS
All sending infrastructure must have the following DNS and mailserver configuration. Failure to do so can result in IPs being listed on the Email Spam IPs (CSS) or compromised IPs (XBL) zones.
Do
- Ensure the sending IP address has a valid reverse DNS (rDNS) entry resolving to a fully qualified domain name (FQDN) for the sending IP address. Spamhaus will treat emails originating from IP addresses without rDNS as suspicious and this will be reflected in the IP's reputation, and receivers using Spamhaus data may subject it to additional filtering.
- Ensure the rDNS hostname resolves to the connecting IP address via a corresponding forward DNS (A/AAAA) record.
- Abusive actors often rely on the reputation of upstream DNS records to hide their identity. Instead, configure a branded reverse DNS to use the sender's own domain, to improve trust signals for the IP address.
Don't
- Do not use generic or auto-generated rDNS entries for dedicated IPs that point to the hosting provider (e.g., static-203-0-113-25.hosting.example.net, 203.113.0.25.broadband.example.net, vps-25.dedicated.hosting.example.com etc). These can negatively impact reputation.
- Do not use random dictionary words in the rDNS and make it identifiable to the sending infrastructure.
How to check
Use the Spamhaus DNS checker tool to check your rDNS configuration.
Do
- Ensure the hostname used in the HELO/EHLO command resolves to the sending IP address.
- Maintain a consistent HELO value that resolves to the sending IP address. Multiple HELO values resolving to different IP addresses may indicate residential proxy and/or malware behaviour.
- Where possible, ensure the HELO/EHLO hostname is consistent with the rDNS hostname.
- Host a webpage on the domain of the HELO, that explains what the domain is for, or that redirects to the main brand domain.
Don't
- Do not use placeholder values such as localhost or generic hostnames that point to the hosting company/ISP as the HELO value.
- Do not resolve HELO hostname to infrastructure that is not used for sending — this behaviour is associated with spoofing and misconfiguration.
- Do not use generic or auto-generated names provided by the hosting provider, use the sender's own domain where possible.
- Do not impersonate the HELO value of well-known mailbox providers like Gmail or Hotmail.
How to check
Enter an IP address into the Spamhaus DNS Checker at the top of this page, to check its HELO value. An email can also be sent to helocheck@abuseat.org to check the HELO being used.
Do
- IPv6 customer allocations must be at least /64 and must have valid reverse DNS. The /64 minimum is consistent with IPv6 subnet architecture and RFC 6177's guidance that email senders should be able to obtain at least a /64. This is further discussed in M3AAWG best practices for IPv6 allocation.
- Add routes for all IP space owned by the sender to reduce vulnerability to BGP hijacking, which can allow hackers to send email that appears to originate from the IP space.
How to check
Run dig -x <an IPv6 address in the allocation> to confirm reverse DNS is present. To confirm the space is actually routed, look the address up at bgp.he.net.
Do
Don't
- Do not allow freemail addresses such as gmail.com or hotmail.com as the 'Envelope FROM.'
- Do not use the NULL envelope sender <> for anything other than indirect out-of-band delivery reports, DSNs and MDNs.
- Do not send bounce messages after accepting unwanted mail. Reject it during the SMTP transaction instead. Bounces sent to forged senders are known as backscatter, which is indirect spam and can severely harm reputation.
How to check
Run dig TXT <envelope sender domain> and confirm an SPF record is returned and includes the sending IPs.
Do
- Audit DNS regularly and remove records for services, hosts and IP space that are no longer used, including CNAMEs, NS delegations, A records and SPF include: entries for former providers.
Don't
- Do not leave records pointing to decommissioned hosts or former providers. Dangling records can be claimed by others and used to send mail that appears to come from the domain.
- Do not use wildcard DNS records.
This article explains domain, hostname terminology and domain alignment in email. Also, use aboutmy.email to check for email configuration setup.
How to check
Run dig against the subdomains and look for CNAMEs that resolve to a provider that no longer serves the domain.
2. Authentication
Authentication is how receiving mail servers verify that emails are authorized to send from the domain. Without SPF, DKIM, and DMARC properly configured, the domain is exposed to spoofing and phishing, and emails are more likely to be rejected or flagged by Spamhaus.
Do
- Publish an SPF TXT record in the domain's DNS zone file that specifies exactly which IPs and hosts are authorized to send email on the domain's behalf.
- Ensure the sending IP is explicitly included in the SPF record. Email sent from IPs not included in SPF will not pass SPF checks.
- Make sure both the HELO domain and the envelope From domain have a valid SPF record. Publish SPF records on this domain (which might be the infrastructure domain) and not the visible header From domain.
- Keep the SPF record within the 10 DNS lookup limit (this includes all nested include: statements). Exceeding the limit returns a PermError, which is not a pass, so SPF cannot authenticate mail or satisfy DMARC alignment.
- Keep the SPF record as narrow as possible. Only include the sending infrastructure actually in use.
Don't
- Do not use overly permissive qualifiers like +all or broad include: ranges that authorise IP space not under the sender's control.
- Do not leave include: statements for providers no longer used for sending. Audit the SPF and remove outdated vendors. Check for typos.
- Avoid using SPF macros unless needed. They are expanded per message at evaluation time, which is costly and makes failures more likely.
- Do not use a or mx mechanisms where ip4: or ip6: would work. Each one costs a DNS lookup against the limit of 10, while ip4: and ip6: cost none.
How to check
Run dig TXT <domain>, then count the mechanisms that trigger a DNS lookup — include, a, mx, ptr, exists and redirect — and confirm the total is 10 or fewer.
Do
- Ensure every outbound message carries a valid DKIM signature, using a minimum 1024-bit key length while 2048-bit is recommended.
- Ensure that the d= domain on the DKIM signature matches the domain on the header From.
- Rotate DKIM keys at least annually, or immediately if a key is suspected to be compromised.
- Use a different d= domain for different mailstreams (for example, separate subdomains for transactional and marketing email), so that each mailstream builds its own reputation.
How to check
Run dig TXT <selector>._domainkey.<domain> (the selector is set in the ESP's DKIM setup page) and confirm a DKIM key, starting v=DKIM1, is returned.
Do
- Publish a DMARC record with a policy defined for the sending domain.
- Ensure the header From domain aligns with the DKIM signing domain (d=) so that DMARC alignment passes.
- Set up a DMARC aggregate report address (rua=) from day one as this will help audit email sent from the domain.
Don't
- Do not remain at p=none permanently. Starting with p=none is acceptable, but we recommend having an enforcement policy.
How to check
Run dig TXT _dmarc.<domain> and confirm a DMARC record, starting v=DMARC1, is returned.
3. Permission and List Hygiene
Send email only to people who want to receive it. Once the technical infrastructure is in place, the next step is building a legitimate list of email addresses from people who have provided explicit permission to receive the email. Lack of permission is one of the most common reasons for being listed by Spamhaus.
Do
- Ensure all bulk email is ONLY sent to recipients that have Confirmed Opt-in (COI). Send a confirmation email requiring recipients to explicitly opt-in to verify their email address. This will prevent unwanted signups, bot signups and typo email addresses. If no opt-in is received, do not send email to that address.
- Utilise available signals like bounce data, feedback loops, postmaster tools and engagement data to ensure the mailing list is up to date and email is sent to an engaged audience.
- Keep a timestamped record of when and how permission was obtained.
Don't
- Do not send emails to purchased, rented, or harvested lists, as these are the most common source of spam trap hits.
- Permission is NOT transferable. Do not grant or assume permission retroactively or transfer it between organisations or domains.
How to check
Look for high bounce rates, low engagement and unusual sign-up patterns in the mailing platform.
Do
- Refer to the guidelines from M3AAWG for managing spamtraps, and follow the best practices outlined in our resources.
- Implement a robust email sunset policy to help remove temporary email sign-ups and email addresses that no longer engage with email.
Don't
- Do not attempt to identify or suppress a spam trap address. Audit the acquisition process to identify which list segment or collection method introduced the problem address, and remove that source entirely.
Spamhaus spamtraps do not subscribe to email or engage with them.
According to M3AAWG spam trap best practices, mailboxes that remain inactive for more than 12 months can be repurposed as spamtraps.
4. Sending best practices
How email is sent matters as much as what is sent. Warming the IP and domain, maintaining a consistent volume, using trusted links and domains within emails, and providing clear, legitimate ways to opt-out of emails will help improve overall deliverability.
Do
- HELO domains which DO NOT have a sending history will be subjected to additional filtering. Please read our best practices around IP/Domain warm-up.
- Start sending slowly, and consistently for any IP address or domain that has not sent email in the past 90 days, before gradually increasing volume.
- Domains which have been registered in the past 24 hours will be part of Spamhaus Zero Reputation Domains (ZRD) list.
- Additionally, domains used for mailing within 30 days of registration will be treated suspiciously and we recommend following best practices for newly registered domains.
- Treat any change in IP or HELO hostname as a new asset if no prior sending history is available, and apply the same warm-up process as used for a new IP or domain.
- Begin with a few initial campaigns sent to the most engaged recipients to reduce the risk of hitting older invalid addresses. Maintaining a slow and consistent email volume will help build a strong sender reputation.
Don't
- Do not use warm-up services that generate artificial traffic or simulate opens, clicks and replies. Using an engagement inflation service will result in the IP or domain being listed.
- Infrastructure operated to inflate engagement or otherwise trick filters will be listed as a spam-enabling service.
- Do not send inconsistent email volumes or trigger a sudden spike in sending, as this could negatively impact reputation.
- Do not send to addresses which are old and unengaged while warming the IP or Domain.
- Do not send the entire daily volume in a single burst at the top of the hour. Spread it across the day as spikes in mail volume can look suspicious.
- Do not use more IPs than required to manage the mail volume as this can be perceived as snowshoe behaviour.
- Do not begin sending on new infrastructure without carrying the suppression list across. Addresses that previously bounced or unsubscribed will otherwise be mailed again, and old inactive addresses are where recycled spam traps sit.
How to check
Plot the daily send volume for the IP or domain against the warm-up schedule and confirm it is increasing gradually, not spiking.
Do
- Keep the overall bounce rate below 5%.
- Suppress hard bounces immediately.
- Investigate and remove repeated soft bounces after a defined threshold; this is typically 3–5 consecutive bounces.
Don't
- Avoid using email list validation as a source to clean spamtraps as it does not do so, and is not and never will be a replacement for permission.
Do
- Bulk commercial senders: Implement the List-Unsubscribe-Post: List-Unsubscribe=One-Click header enabling one-click unsubscribe directly from the inbox (RFC 8058).
- Include a clearly visible unsubscribe link in the body of every commercial email.
- Action unsubscribe requests within 2 days and add them to a suppression list.
Don't
- Do not hide or obfuscate unsubscribe links.
- Do not require recipients to authenticate to unsubscribe.
- Avoid use of one-click unsubscribe in the body of an email; instead, make sure the link leads to a confirmation page.
How to check
Send a test campaign to a test mailbox, open the message headers (e.g. Gmail's "Show original"), and confirm that List-Unsubscribe and List-Unsubscribe-Post are both present. Also check that all links in the email work.
Do
- Use HTTPS for all links, and only use links generated by the sender's own system.
- Sign or validate tracking and redirect links so they cannot be altered to point elsewhere. This prevents malicious actors from abusing them as open redirects.
Don't
- Do not use free or unbranded URL shorteners in the content of an email. URLs and/or domains used in the content of an email will affect the overall reputation of the sending domain.
5. IP and Domain Reputation
The reputation of the IP and domain as seen by Spamhaus can be checked via our reputation checker.
Spamhaus looks at multiple signals before assigning a reputation score, and a strong negative signal can outweigh the absence of positive ones — so following all email best practices consistently is essential.
Factors that influence reputation include: the service provider, the IP neighbourhood, the infrastructure the IPs are associated with, the upstream networks that connect to internet backbones, and the IP or domain's history — when it was first seen, when it was last used, and how it was used.
Do
- Check the IP reputation and domain reputation regularly and do not wait for a delivery issue or listing to discover an issue.
- Associate the domain with network providers and registrars that maintain a good reputation. The reputation of the hosting provider or registrar can be checked on our reputation statistics page.
- Ensure newly registered domains are not used for at least 30 days from registration. The domain can be used for non-email purposes during this period, and establishing a web-presence prior to sending email will help improve the credibility of the domain.
- Refer to our recommendations for best practices when using newly registered domains.
Don't
- Do not use newly registered domains in SMTP as a FROM domain or a HELO domain unless the domain is properly warmed up. Similarly, using a newly registered domain in the content of the email can also look suspicious. The age of the domains used in the email can affect the overall sending reputation.
- Do not use cousin domains for additional mailstreams or geographies for the same brand. Use sub-domains.
- Do not hide WHOIS information for the root sending domain. The reputation of the upstream provider may be used for evaluating domain reputation. The reputation of the upstream provider can be checked in our Registrar reputation page.
How to check
Run the domain through the Reputation Checker to get more insights.
Note: We do not accept requests for explanations of the attributes shown here or requests to reset reputation.
6. ESPs & Large Senders
ESPs and shared infrastructure hosts are responsible for the email sent via their infrastructure. Hosting abusive senders will negatively impact the reputation of shared domains and infrastructure.
