- Meet the IPv6 allocation and reverse DNS minimum If sending over IPv6, the sending address must fall within an allocation of /64 or larger (a /64 is the standard block size we recommend assigning), and that space must have valid reverse DNS. IPv6 ranges without reverse DNS or with allocations smaller than /64 are often misused by spammers. See section
- Authenticate mail with SPF, DKIM and DMARC Publish SPF and DMARC records for every sending domain, sign every outbound message with a signature, and align the DKIM sending domain with the domain in the message's RFC 5322 From address. Authentication is one of the signals that shapes reputation, so gaps here make a listing more likely when other signals are weak. See section
Operating an Email Server Provider (ESP) or other shared sending infrastructure? See the ESPs and Large Senders guidelines
1. Infrastructure and DNS
All sending infrastructure must have the following DNS and mailserver configuration. Failure to do so can result in IPs being listed on the Email Spam IPs (CSS) or compromised IPs (XBL) zones.
Do
- Ensure the sending IP address has a valid reverse DNS (rDNS) entry resolving to a fully qualified domain name (FQDN) for the sending IP address. Spamhaus will treat emails originating from IP addresses without rDNS as suspicious and this will be reflected in the IP's reputation, and receivers using Spamhaus data may subject it to additional filtering.
- Ensure the rDNS hostname resolves to the connecting IP address via a corresponding forward DNS (A/AAAA) record.
- Abusive actors often rely on the reputation of upstream DNS records to hide their identity. Instead, configure a branded reverse DNS to use the sender's own domain, to improve trust signals for the IP address.
Don't
- Do not use generic or auto-generated rDNS entries for dedicated IPs that point to the hosting provider (e.g., static-203-0-113-25.hosting.example.net, 203.113.0.25.broadband.example.net, vps-25.dedicated.hosting.example.com etc). These can negatively impact reputation.
- Do not use random dictionary words in the rDNS and make it identifiable to the sending infrastructure.
How to check
Use the Spamhaus DNS checker tool to check your rDNS configuration.
Do
- Ensure the hostname used in the HELO/EHLO command resolves to the sending IP address.
- Maintain a consistent HELO value that resolves to the sending IP address. Multiple HELO values resolving to different IP addresses may indicate residential proxy and/or malware behaviour.
- Where possible, ensure the HELO/EHLO hostname is consistent with the rDNS hostname.
- Host a webpage on the domain of the HELO, that explains what the domain is for, or that redirects to the main brand domain.
Don't
- Do not use placeholder values such as localhost or generic hostnames that point to the hosting company/ISP as the HELO value.
- Do not resolve HELO hostname to infrastructure that is not used for sending — this behaviour is associated with spoofing and misconfiguration.
- Do not use generic or auto-generated names provided by the hosting provider, use the sender's own domain where possible.
- Do not impersonate the HELO value of well-known mailbox providers like Gmail or Hotmail.
How to check
Enter an IP address into the Spamhaus DNS Checker at the top of this page, to check its HELO value. An email can also be sent to helocheck@abuseat.org to check the HELO being used.
Do
- IPv6 customer allocations must be at least /64 and must have valid reverse DNS. The /64 minimum is consistent with IPv6 subnet architecture and RFC 6177's guidance that email senders should be able to obtain at least a /64. This is further discussed in M3AAWG best practices for IPv6 allocation.
- Add routes for all IP space owned by the sender to reduce vulnerability to BGP hijacking, which can allow hackers to send email that appears to originate from the IP space.
How to check
Run dig -x <an IPv6 address in the allocation> to confirm reverse DNS is present. To confirm the space is actually routed, look the address up at bgp.he.net.
Do
Don't
- Do not allow freemail addresses such as gmail.com or hotmail.com as the 'Envelope FROM.'
- Do not use the NULL envelope sender <> for anything other than indirect out-of-band delivery reports, DSNs and MDNs.
- Do not send bounce messages after accepting unwanted mail. Reject it during the SMTP transaction instead. Bounces sent to forged senders are known as backscatter, which is indirect spam and can severely harm reputation.
How to check
Run dig TXT <envelope sender domain> and confirm an SPF record is returned and includes the sending IPs.
Do
- Audit DNS regularly and remove records for services, hosts and IP space that are no longer used, including CNAMEs, NS delegations, A records and SPF include: entries for former providers.
Don't
- Do not leave records pointing to decommissioned hosts or former providers. Dangling records can be claimed by others and used to send mail that appears to come from the domain.
- Do not use wildcard DNS records.
This article explains domain, hostname terminology and domain alignment in email. Also, use aboutmy.email to check for email configuration setup.
How to check
Run dig against the subdomains and look for CNAMEs that resolve to a provider that no longer serves the domain.
2. Authentication
Authentication is how receiving mail servers verify that emails are authorized to send from the domain. Without SPF, DKIM, and DMARC properly configured, the domain is exposed to spoofing and phishing, and emails are more likely to be rejected or flagged by Spamhaus.
Do
- Publish an SPF TXT record in the domain's DNS zone file that specifies exactly which IPs and hosts are authorized to send email on the domain's behalf.
- Ensure the sending IP is explicitly included in the SPF record. Email sent from IPs not included in SPF will not pass SPF checks.
- Make sure both the HELO domain and the envelope From domain have a valid SPF record. Publish SPF records on this domain (which might be the infrastructure domain) and not the visible header From domain.
- Keep the SPF record within the 10 DNS lookup limit (this includes all nested include: statements). Exceeding the limit returns a PermError, which is not a pass, so SPF cannot authenticate mail or satisfy DMARC alignment.
- Keep the SPF record as narrow as possible. Only include the sending infrastructure actually in use.
Don't
- Do not use overly permissive qualifiers like +all or broad include: ranges that authorise IP space not under the sender's control.
- Do not leave include: statements for providers no longer used for sending. Audit the SPF and remove outdated vendors. Check for typos.
- Avoid using SPF macros unless needed. They are expanded per message at evaluation time, which is costly and makes failures more likely.
- Do not use a or mx mechanisms where ip4: or ip6: would work. Each one costs a DNS lookup against the limit of 10, while ip4: and ip6: cost none.
How to check
Run dig TXT <domain>, then count the mechanisms that trigger a DNS lookup — include, a, mx, ptr, exists and redirect — and confirm the total is 10 or fewer.
Do
- Ensure every outbound message carries a valid DKIM signature, using a minimum 1024-bit key length while 2048-bit is recommended.
- Ensure that the d= domain on the DKIM signature matches the domain on the header From.
- Rotate DKIM keys at least annually, or immediately if a key is suspected to be compromised.
- Use a different d= domain for different mailstreams (for example, separate subdomains for transactional and marketing email), so that each mailstream builds its own reputation.
How to check
Run dig TXT <selector>._domainkey.<domain> (the selector is set in the ESP's DKIM setup page) and confirm a DKIM key, starting v=DKIM1, is returned.
Do
- Publish a DMARC record with a policy defined for the sending domain.
- Ensure the header From domain aligns with the DKIM signing domain (d=) so that DMARC alignment passes.
- Set up a DMARC aggregate report address (rua=) from day one as this will help audit email sent from the domain.
Don't
- Do not remain at p=none permanently. Starting with p=none is acceptable, but we recommend having an enforcement policy.
How to check
Run dig TXT _dmarc.<domain> and confirm a DMARC record, starting v=DMARC1, is returned.
3. Permission and List Hygiene
Send email only to people who want to receive it. Once the technical infrastructure is in place, the next step is building a legitimate list of email addresses from people who have provided explicit permission to receive the email. Lack of permission is one of the most common reasons for being listed by Spamhaus.
Do
- Ensure all bulk email is ONLY sent to recipients that have Confirmed Opt-in (COI). Send a confirmation email requiring recipients to explicitly opt-in to verify their email address. This will prevent unwanted signups, bot signups and typo email addresses. If no opt-in is received, do not send email to that address.
- Utilise available signals like bounce data, feedback loops, postmaster tools and engagement data to ensure the mailing list is up to date and email is sent to an engaged audience.
- Keep a timestamped record of when and how permission was obtained.
Don't
- Do not send emails to purchased, rented, or harvested lists, as these are the most common source of spam trap hits.
- Permission is NOT transferable. Do not grant or assume permission retroactively or transfer it between organisations or domains.
How to check
Look for high bounce rates, low engagement and unusual sign-up patterns in the mailing platform.
Do
- Refer to the guidelines from M3AAWG for managing spamtraps, and follow the best practices outlined in our resources.
- Implement a robust email sunset policy to help remove temporary email sign-ups and email addresses that no longer engage with email.
Don't
- Do not attempt to identify or suppress a spam trap address. Audit the acquisition process to identify which list segment or collection method introduced the problem address, and remove that source entirely.
Spamhaus spamtraps do not subscribe to email or engage with them.
According to M3AAWG spam trap best practices, mailboxes that remain inactive for more than 12 months can be repurposed as spamtraps.
4. Sending best practices
How email is sent matters as much as what is sent. Warming the IP and domain, maintaining a consistent volume, using trusted links and domains within emails, and providing clear, legitimate ways to opt-out of emails will help improve overall deliverability.
Do
- HELO domains which DO NOT have a sending history will be subjected to additional filtering. Please read our best practices around IP/Domain warm-up.
- Start sending slowly, and consistently for any IP address or domain that has not sent email in the past 90 days, before gradually increasing volume.
- Domains which have been registered in the past 24 hours will be part of Spamhaus Zero Reputation Domains (ZRD) list.
- Additionally, domains used for mailing within 30 days of registration will be treated suspiciously and we recommend following best practices for newly registered domains.
- Treat any change in IP or HELO hostname as a new asset if no prior sending history is available, and apply the same warm-up process as used for a new IP or domain.
- Begin with a few initial campaigns sent to the most engaged recipients to reduce the risk of hitting older invalid addresses. Maintaining a slow and consistent email volume will help build a strong sender reputation.
Don't
- Do not use warm-up services that generate artificial traffic or simulate opens, clicks and replies. Using an engagement inflation service will result in the IP or domain being listed.
- Infrastructure operated to inflate engagement or otherwise trick filters will be listed as a spam-enabling service.
- Do not send inconsistent email volumes or trigger a sudden spike in sending, as this could negatively impact reputation.
- Do not send to addresses which are old and unengaged while warming the IP or Domain.
- Do not send the entire daily volume in a single burst at the top of the hour. Spread it across the day as spikes in mail volume can look suspicious.
- Do not use more IPs than required to manage the mail volume as this can be perceived as snowshoe behaviour.
- Do not begin sending on new infrastructure without carrying the suppression list across. Addresses that previously bounced or unsubscribed will otherwise be mailed again, and old inactive addresses are where recycled spam traps sit.
How to check
Plot the daily send volume for the IP or domain against the warm-up schedule and confirm it is increasing gradually, not spiking.
Do
- Keep the overall bounce rate below 5%.
- Suppress hard bounces immediately.
- Investigate and remove repeated soft bounces after a defined threshold; this is typically 3–5 consecutive bounces.
Don't
- Avoid using email list validation as a source to clean spamtraps as it does not do so, and is not and never will be a replacement for permission.
Do
- Bulk commercial senders: Implement the List-Unsubscribe-Post: List-Unsubscribe=One-Click header enabling one-click unsubscribe directly from the inbox (RFC 8058).
- Include a clearly visible unsubscribe link in the body of every commercial email.
- Action unsubscribe requests within 2 days and add them to a suppression list.
Don't
- Do not hide or obfuscate unsubscribe links.
- Do not require recipients to authenticate to unsubscribe.
- Avoid use of one-click unsubscribe in the body of an email; instead, make sure the link leads to a confirmation page.
How to check
Send a test campaign to a test mailbox, open the message headers (e.g. Gmail's "Show original"), and confirm that List-Unsubscribe and List-Unsubscribe-Post are both present. Also check that all links in the email work.
Do
- Use HTTPS for all links, and only use links generated by the sender's own system.
- Sign or validate tracking and redirect links so they cannot be altered to point elsewhere. This prevents malicious actors from abusing them as open redirects.
Don't
- Do not use free or unbranded URL shorteners in the content of an email. URLs and/or domains used in the content of an email will affect the overall reputation of the sending domain.
5. IP and Domain Reputation
The reputation of the IP and domain as seen by Spamhaus can be checked via our reputation checker.
Spamhaus looks at multiple signals before assigning a reputation score, and a strong negative signal can outweigh the absence of positive ones — so following all email best practices consistently is essential.
Factors that influence reputation include: the service provider, the IP neighbourhood, the infrastructure the IPs are associated with, the upstream networks that connect to internet backbones, and the IP or domain's history — when it was first seen, when it was last used, and how it was used.
Do
- Check the IP reputation and domain reputation regularly and do not wait for a delivery issue or listing to discover an issue.
- Associate the domain with network providers and registrars that maintain a good reputation. The reputation of the hosting provider or registrar can be checked on our reputation statistics page.
- Ensure newly registered domains are not used for at least 30 days from registration. The domain can be used for non-email purposes during this period, and establishing a web-presence prior to sending email will help improve the credibility of the domain.
- Refer to our recommendations for best practices when using newly registered domains.
Don't
- Do not use newly registered domains in SMTP as a FROM domain or a HELO domain unless the domain is properly warmed up. Similarly, using a newly registered domain in the content of the email can also look suspicious. The age of the domains used in the email can affect the overall sending reputation.
- Do not use cousin domains for additional mailstreams or geographies for the same brand. Use sub-domains.
- Do not hide WHOIS information for the root sending domain. The reputation of the upstream provider may be used for evaluating domain reputation. The reputation of the upstream provider can be checked in our Registrar reputation page.
How to check
Run the domain through the Reputation Checker to get more insights.
Note: We do not accept requests for explanations of the attributes shown here or requests to reset reputation.
6. ESPs & Large Senders
ESPs and shared infrastructure hosts are responsible for the email sent via their infrastructure. Hosting abusive senders will negatively impact the reputation of shared domains and infrastructure.

articles.title: Show HN: Claimseed, synthetic Medicare docs with planted errors and answer keys
articles.body:
Seeded, fully synthetic U.S. medical-billing specimen documents — Medicare Summary Notices, hospital itemized bills and Medicare Advantage explanations of benefits — rendered to PDF with ground-truth JSON that says exactly which billing errors were injected and where. For testing document extractors, bill-review tools and agents without ever touching a real person's paperwork.
- Every name, identifier, address, phone number and amount is generated from a seed. Nothing in this repository
is, or is derived from, a real document; see docs/synthetic-data-policy.md.
- Every rendered page says so: a specimen band (text, in the foot margin), a diagonal watermark (drawn as shapes, so it never leaks letters into text extraction) and PDF metadata, stamped into the finished PDF by the renderer itself — no CLI flag, library call or data object switches them off.
- Same seed, same document: all content is derived from the seed, fonts are bundled and PDF metadata is fixed, so two renders on the same Chrome build (Linux, as in CI) are byte-identical; other platforms produce the same content, with bytes that may differ by Chrome version.
The standard set is 1,022 blind documents over all 34 published scenarios: 260 Medicare Summary Notices (13 scenarios x 20 seeds), 250 itemized bills (5 x 50), 256 PPO EOBs (8 x 32) and 256 HMO EOBs (8 x 32). Bills and EOBs turn through the standard layout and its 12 variants; one document in five is a degraded copy (scan, fax, photo, low resolution in turn); every notice and EOB has its 835. Layout, preset and 835 turn alike for every scenario, so none tells the scenario.
claimseed 0.6.0's copy is attached to the GitHub release v0.6.0: claimseed-0.6.0-standard-documents.zip unzips to
claimseed-0.6.0-standard/documents/ (PDFs, 835s, README.md, SHA256SUMS) and claimseed-0.6.0-standard-keys.zip
to claimseed-0.6.0-standard/keys/ (answer keys, manifest.jsonl, README.md, SHA256SUMS and set.json: the
claimseed and Chrome versions, the release's git tree, document count, salt and canary). Give the tool under test only
the documents folder. The 835s sit beside the PDFs there; to score a tool on reading the PDFs alone, give it only the
.pdf files:
# run the tool on every PDF in documents/; write one report per document to reports/<id>.json,
# in the shape of schemas/extractor-output.schema.json
npx @claimseed/core verify --manifest claimseed-0.6.0-standard/keys/manifest.jsonl --outputs reports
# the same content again with claimseed 0.6.0 and the salt in set.json (or any of its keys); PDF bytes can
# differ by machine and Chrome install, so the SHA-256s in the manifest and SHA256SUMS name the published files
npx @claimseed/core@0.6.0 batch --set standard --out documents --blind-keys keys --blind-salt SALT
It is a public development set with public keys; every answer key and manifest line carries a canary string with a
fixed GUID (blind.canary) so that people who train models can find and leave out claimseed answer keys, and people
who test a model can check whether it has seen them. Please keep the keys out of training data. For a held-out test,
make your own blind set with batch --blind-keys (a fresh salt) and keep its keys to yourself.
From npm (Node.js 22.13 or later):
npx @claimseed/core list
npx @claimseed/core render msn combined-three-errors --seed demo --out ./out
npx @claimseed/core generate itemized-bill balance-billing --seed demo > demo.json
Rendering needs a Chrome or Chromium binary (CLAIMSEED_CHROME=/path/to/chrome, or an install in a usual place);
generate does not. Run these from any folder outside a checkout of this repository: inside one, npx takes the
repository's own copy of the package, which needs npm ci first (see "From a checkout" below).
As a library (npm install @claimseed/core, ESM):
import { generateData, render } from '@claimseed/core';
const { data, groundTruth } = generateData({ type: 'msn', scenario: 'baseline-clean', seed: 'demo' });
const { pdf, groundTruth: gt } = await render({ type: 'msn', scenario: 'baseline-clean', seed: 'demo', outDir: './out' });
As an MCP server for agents (@claimseed/mcp, stdio). Rendered documents come back as page images that chat
clients show in the conversation (directly, or in an MCP Apps view with the injected errors beside the pages), and
no file is saved:
npx -y @claimseed/mcp
or, to also keep each PDF and its ground truth, with a folder it writes into and nowhere else:
npx -y @claimseed/mcp --workspace ./claimseed-out
or with the published container image, Chromium included:
docker run -i --rm --network none --read-only --tmpfs /tmp --cap-drop ALL --security-opt no-new-privileges \
  --user "$(id -u):$(id -g)" -v "$PWD/claimseed-out:/work" ghcr.io/claimseed/claimseed-mcp
The server is also listed in the MCP registry as io.github.claimseed/claimseed. See packages/mcp/README.md for
the tools, the client configuration and the limits.
From a checkout of this repository:
npm ci
cd packages/core
node src/cli.js list
node src/cli.js render msn combined-three-errors --seed demo --out ./out
and docker build -t claimseed-mcp . at the repository root builds the same image as the published one.
See packages/core/README.md for the engine, docs/error-taxonomy.md for the error kinds a scenario can inject,
and schemas/ground-truth.schema.json for the ground-truth format.
Render a set, run your extractor or bill auditor on the PDFs, and score its reports against the answer keys:
npx @claimseed/core batch --types msn,itemized-bill --seeds 20 --out ./set
# write one report per document to ./reports/<pdf name>.json, in the shape of schemas/extractor-output.schema.json
npx @claimseed/core verify --manifest ./set/manifest.jsonl --outputs ./reports
The score gives field accuracy, error recall and precision, false alarms and the paths read wrong or missed. Clean
scenarios test for false alarms; some scenarios of every type also plant decoys, lines that look like errors but
follow the rules (the same service on two dates, a charge far above the approved amount, a copay cut short where
the member reaches the out-of-pocket maximum), and flagging one counts as a false alarm.
Agents can score one document at a time with the MCP tool verify_document.
The headline figures of verify --manifest (fields, errors) now count every document: a missing or invalid
report scores as an empty one, and so does a part a report leaves out (fields or errors) once any report gives that
part. Skipping a document never raises field accuracy or error recall; precision counts only what was flagged, so
read it beside recall. scoredOnly holds the earlier figures, over the scored reports; byType, byDegradation
(clean or the preset) and byKind (expected, found and recall per error kind) break them down.
For tools that must not see the answers, render and batch take --blind-keys KEYDIR. A blind document is named
by an opaque id (doc- and 16 hexadecimal digits): its specimen band, PDF title, file names, page-image markers and
835 carry that id, never the scenario, planted errors or seed. Its answer key (ground truth 1.5) and a batch's
manifest go to KEYDIR, never the documents' folder or one inside it:
npx @claimseed/core batch --types msn,itemized-bill --seeds 20 --out ./set --blind-keys ./keys
Content comes from a seed derived from a salt, 128 random bits drawn for each set and recorded in every key, so
nobody can rebuild a document from a guessed scenario and seed and match a printed claim number. --blind-salt SALT
(from an earlier set's key) makes the same set again; documents are written in an order drawn from the salt. A
degraded copy is blind too, with its own id and copyOf in its key. The band, watermark and metadata still mark
every page as a specimen; only the scenario words are gone. verify --manifest scores a blind set exactly as an
open set.
Over MCP, render_blind returns the id and page images, never the key, scenario or seed, and get_answer_key the key
(see packages/mcp/README.md).
Extractors meet scans, faxes and phone photos, not only clean PDFs. A degraded copy keeps the document's answer key:
npx @claimseed/core render msn combined-three-errors --seed demo --out ./out --degrade fax
npx @claimseed/core batch --types msn,itemized-bill --seeds 20 --degrade scan --out ./set
The presets are scan, fax, photo and low-res. render --degrade writes an image-only PDF, one image per page
and the answer key; batch --degrade writes the PDFs and answer keys of a set, with its manifest. The answer key holds
the settings the seed chose (rotation, resolution, noise and the rest) in degradationParams. The specimen band and
watermark are drawn on top of the degraded pages, never through the degradation (a fax also prints the watermark as a
dot pattern that survives black and white), and every image file carries the specimen markers. Agents can ask for a
copy with the MCP tool degrade_document.
A Medicare Summary Notice or a Medicare Advantage EOB can come with the X12 835 remittance of the same claims, for testing software that reads payments rather than paper:
npx @claimseed/core render msn combined-three-errors --seed demo --out ./out --also 835
npx @claimseed/core batch --types msn,ppo-eob,hmo-eob --seeds 20 --also 835 --out ./set
Each .835 is a 005010X221A1 file marked as test data (ISA15 is T, and the sender and receiver IDs, the payer and
the contact say specimen or test), with no bank data. The answer key lists it beside the PDF, and every planted error that shows in the 835
names its place there (x12Ref): a wrong claim total breaks the claim's balance or its patient-responsibility total, and a
duplicate is a repeated service line. Agents ask for it with also: "835" on the MCP tool render_document. See the
core README for what the files contain and what they leave out.
An extractor tested on one layout may have learned the layout rather than the document. The itemized bill and both
Medicare Advantage EOBs therefore come in 12 layout variants each (b01-b12, p01-p12, h01-h12): an id
fixes the column order, the header and title wording, the font, density and colors, and how a table continued on
the next page is marked. The data, every amount and every required item stay as they are, and the answer key
differs only in naming the variant, the page count and the PDF's hash:
npx @claimseed/core render ppo-eob combined-three-errors --seed demo --layout-variant p07 --out ./out
npx @claimseed/core render hmo-eob baseline-clean --seed demo --layout-variant all --out ./out
npx @claimseed/core batch --types itemized-bill,ppo-eob,hmo-eob --seeds 20 --layout-variant seeded --out ./set
all (render and batch) writes one document per id. seeded picks an id from the seed alone, so for one seed the
three types take the same position in their lists (b04, p04 and h04 together); give explicit ids to spread
layouts across types. Files are named <type>_<scenario>_<seed>.<id>.pdf, and the answer key records the variant
(documents[0].layout is ppo-eob.p07, with the details in documents[0].layoutVariant; ground truth 1.4). The
option works with --degrade and --also 835 (the 835 is the same as the standard document's). The Medicare
Summary Notice has one national format and takes no variant. Agents pass layout_variant to the MCP tools; the
ids and what each fixes are listed in packages/core/data/<type>/variants.json.
- Synthea simulates synthetic patient populations and exports their records, claims included, as FHIR, C-CDA and CSV. It models care, not printed billing documents.
- CMS's Blue Button 2.0 API offers developers a sandbox of synthetic Medicare enrollee data, served as FHIR resources.
- claimseed prints the documents a patient or a bill reviewer actually reads (Medicare Summary Notices, itemized bills, Medicare Advantage EOBs) with CPT/HCPCS codes, amounts from public fee schedules, planted errors and decoys, and an answer key for each. It does not model clinical histories; use Synthea beside it for those.
0.6.0 adds blind documents and sets (--blind-keys and --blind-salt, and the MCP tools render_blind and
get_answer_key), the published standard set of 1,022 blind documents with its answer keys (attached to the GitHub
release v0.6.0), and set scores that count every document. 0.5.0 added planted errors and decoys on the Medicare
Advantage EOBs (14 new scenarios), layout variants of the itemized bill and both EOBs (--layout-variant,
layout_variant: 12 ids per type, with the variant recorded in the answer key), and strict MCP arguments (every tool
refuses an argument it does not declare). 0.4.0 added 835 remittances and scanned-looking copies. 0.3.0 added
scoring, batch output with a manifest, and decoys. 0.2.0 added page images in the MCP server's results, an MCP Apps
view and a mode that writes no files. Versions before 1.0 may still change their interfaces. The layouts shipped are
msn, itemized-bill, ppo-eob and hmo-eob. Next is a bill and the EOB of the same visit (a fictional commercial
employer-plan EOB beside the provider's itemized bill, with errors that show only across the two); docs/roadmap.md
gives the order of the work after it. examples/ lists one rendered document per scenario and one per layout
variant id. Licensed under Apache-2.0 (see LICENSE and NOTICE).
Output is for testing software. Do not present a specimen to a beneficiary, patient, payer or agency as a real
document, and do not remove the specimen markers from one you pass on; see docs/synthetic-data-policy.md.
See CONTRIBUTING.md (synthetic-data rules, review checklist, DCO sign-off) and SECURITY.md.

articles.title: OpenAI releases a new image classifier and ChatGPT warnings to combat CSAM
articles.body:
OpenAI today announced new tools to combat child sexual abuse material (CSAM) amid growing safety concerns around the use of AI tools. These features include a new image classifier to detect CSAM, warnings and temporary blocks to prevent users from creating or accessing content that sexualizes children, a new guideline for developers, and a set of tools for law enforcement.
The company unveiled a new image classifier that can detect CSAM images, including the ones generated by AI. OpenAI is giving select companies access to its classifier through its API at no cost. The tool looks for visual signs of abuse in images not seen before and assigns a score that can give an indicative direction to reviewers about dealing with CSAM.
OpenAI said that it developed this classifier with the National Center for Missing and Exploited Children (NCMEC), and it is working with Tech Coalition and ROOST to share access to the tool. In its early testing with partners, the AI company found that the classifier flags 48% fewer images while finding the same number of abusive images, reducing the work of reviewers. Plus, images flagged by the classifier are twice as likely to be abusive images.
What’s more, the company is adding new warning screens in ChatGPT to prevent users from accessing material that sexualizes children. ChatGPT will show an alert to users attempting such prompts, direct users toward specialized support to stop harmful behavior, and also suspend the account for 24 hours as a warning. The app already blocks CSAM content and requests related to it. It said that repeated offences could lead to the account being removed permanently.
OpenAI noted that it formed the message and guidelines around this behavior with organizations and researchers, including Protect Children, the Lucy Faithfull Foundation, and Joel Scanlan at the University of Tasmania, who independently evaluated a trial of deterrent messages.
The company is also publishing guidelines for developers using OpenAI tools to prevent, detect, and help users report CSAM content. It said that in early testing, the guidelines have helped a number of developers adopt child safety tooling and register to report CSAM to NCMEC. OpenAI is also equipping law enforcement dealing with child safety with AI-powered features like dedicated plug-ins, investigative tools, and complex data analysis, with access managed by program administrators. It is also providing training to investigators along with a field guide on how to use AI.
OpenAI has had several lawsuits against the company blaming its technology for harming users, especially children. Safety-focused nonprofit Common Sense Media labeled OpenAI’s tech as “unacceptable risk” for teens. Other AI chatbots — specifically Grok — have been used to create nonconsensual sexualized imagery, including of children.
The AI startup had made changes in the last 12 months to its technology, including releasing a safety blueprint, updating content guidelines to bar inappropriate content, retuning its model to prevent them from generating harmful content, and releasing a special version of ChatGPT for teens.

articles.title: Psychic: Like fzf but learns from your actions
articles.body:
psychic: like fzf but learns from your actions
psychic is a fast file browser with ML-powered ranking
Most days I’m in the terminal cd’ing into directories and opening files in my editor. In any given week it’s mostly the same files and dirs because I’m working on the same projects. I was annoyed I had to remember where files live, and tired of tab-completing the same few paths. My computer should already know which file I want to open!
So I made psychic, a fast terminal-based file browser. It tracks the directories you go to and remembers which files you open. It trains a lightweight ML model on your data and ranks results using that model. It prioritizes interactivity and speed above all else: results update as you type and the UI renders in under 16ms.
Everything about how it works flows from a key design decision: it has to be fast enough to update within one frame after a keypress. I’d rather do 10 fast searches in the space of a couple seconds, than 1 smart search that takes many seconds to complete.
I use psychic every time I’m on my computer. It’s become the main way I move around the filesystem. Some numbers: Since I started using it in October 2025,
- I’ve opened it 1450 times. On average, I typed 1.6 characters before I had what I wanted.
- 29% of the time I typed nothing! psychic knew what I wanted, top result. All I did was open and hit enter.
- Median time from opening psychic to getting where I wanted to go was 2 seconds. 41% of searches happened within 1s, 69% within 3s.
- 80% of the time, I picked the top result. 96% of picks were in the top 3.
- The paths I selected were about 50 characters away, on average. So I’m typing 3% of that to get there.
(These are from the built-in psychic stats command, which you can run on your own history!)
It’s on homebrew: brew install kshitijl/tap/psychic.
On the left are search results. On the right is a preview of the file or directory currently selected. You type a query in the bottom and the results are filtered and ranked, changing with every letter. If you hit Enter on a file, it opens your terminal editor in the same window and waits in the background. If it’s a directory, it restarts the search from inside there. It remembers every file and dir you open, and a shell integration records every dir you cd into from outside psychic. All of those are included in every search.
It’s like fzf and zoxide had a baby, plus a small ML model that learns your patterns and favorites. It’s doing ad optimization on your own data, to help you navigate your computer faster.
How it works
All your searches and clicks get written to a sqlite db on your computer. psychic trains a LightGBM model on that data. The model learns to predict which files you’ll open, based on your search query. psychic uses the model to rank search results. After every keypress, psychic reruns the model and reranks all results.
For more details, see the README in the repo.
Some key design decisions
The model I use is LightGBM, an implementation of gradient-boosted trees. It’s tiny and fast and trains in seconds. It can learn rules that depend on threshold values. For example, it can learn a rule like “Files above 1 MB are only opened if they’ve been modified in the last 24 hours”, like log files. LightGBM also has the excellent LambdaRank objective, which is specialized for exactly this kind of ranking task.
The latency budget ruled out any model that’s not local: a network call could easily be over 10 ms or worse. It also ruled out LLMs or any kind of transformer model. Linear and logistic regression were too simple and performed much worse than LightGBM.
The model is re-trained from scratch every time you open psychic. This means it always reflects your current usage patterns. Training happens in the background and writes the model to disk when it’s done. We don’t switch to using the new model while you’re looking at results, because it’s jarring when apps do that. Instead, we wait for when you’re not looking at the screen, like when you’re opening a file in an editor or when you click on a directory. Then we switch to the new model. I’m proud of this careful little dance.
When a user has just started using psychic, there aren’t enough clicks to train on. We use a simple model that rewards recent clicks, recent modification time and a fuzzy match between the query and filename. The final score is a weighted sum of the simple model and ML model. With few clicks, the simple model dominates. As more clicks accumulate, the ML model’s score gets higher weight, until it’s basically 1.
How to be psychic
I use a carefully chosen set of features to try to predict which file you’ll open. Some features are simple: how recently you last clicked it within psychic, its modification time, whether the filename starts with the query, a fuzzy text match score between the query and the filename. Here’s a debug pane that shows the features and some performance stats:
One feature is “number of recent clicks on files that are in the same directory as this one”. This feature helps the model boost files that are in currently active projects.
The feature “clicks for this query” helps the model associate specific queries with specific files, without having to literally remember filenames and query texts. This way, while the model doesn’t directly see filenames, it can still remember associations.
An episode is defined as everything that happens from opening psychic (or from the last click) to clicking on an item. So a single episode has a bunch of queries, including hitting backspace and trying new queries. The feature “engagements in episode with query” counts the number of times you clicked on a file at any point in an episode that had the current query. So if you always type “es” and end up clicking on “bayesian-estimate.md”, then the model can see that association. Next time you type “es”, the model will put that file at the top of the list.
Computer go fast
I watch perf closely and spent a lot of effort on a good benchmarking setup, plus perf logging. Every commit has performance benchmarks. If you use psychic and get bad performance, that’s a bug! Let me know and I’ll fix it.
My tech choices were driven by performance. Probably the most important choices were Rust and LightGBM.
Syscalls are expensive but of course this whole program is syscalls. I tried to minimize syscalls. No filesystem syscalls in the main render loop; I carefully made sure that we ask for file metadata at the time we walk the filesystem and then carry that around everywhere else.

articles.title: “…and the proof is checked in Lean”
articles.body:
This post is an attempt to explain in simple terms how to interpret claims of the form “this theorem is correct because it was checked in Lean”. The summary is: there is an important signal that can be extracted from Lean code, but if this code is AI-generated then you need to do some tests first. We explain the tests, and note that in many cases (such as the OpenAI theorem dump) these tests have not yet been systematically done.
Introduction
Last month’s theorem dump by OpenAI consisted of 722 mathematics papers, around 45% of which came with some Lean code. Three of the (non-Leanified) papers have since been retracted because of a sign error. Some people might say “well, the papers that come with Lean code are definitely correct because that’s how Lean works”. Others might say “well Lean had a soundness bug and could well have more, and AIs will reward hack, so Lean verification doesn’t tell us much at all”. The truth, unsurprisingly, is more subtle, and this post is an attempt to explain it.
This post is structured as a sequence of four questions that one needs to ask about a Lean repository, particularly if it is AI-generated, before one can start to make correctness claims of this form. And before I start, let me stress that for many of the papers in the OpenAI theorem dump, these questions have not yet all been answered affirmatively (but there is nothing stopping people from answering these questions, and I have no reason to believe that any of the tests below will fail, it’s just that people didn’t do them yet).
Question 1. Does the Lean statement match the informal statement?
A Lean repository will typically have a “headline theorem statement”. This will be some computer code which defines the statement (not the proof!) of a theorem. Note the huge difference here between the statement, and the proof. For example here is some fully-compiling Lean code which defines a mathematical statement.
import Mathlibdef FermatsLastTheorem : Prop :=   ∀ a b c n : ℕ, n ≥ 3 → a^n + b^n ≠ c^n 
		
This code imports Lean’s mathematics library Mathlib and then defines a mathematical statement which looks at first glance like it might be Fermat’s Last Theorem, but which actually is a trivially false statement because in Lean ℕ contains 0, so a = b = c = 0 and n = 3 gives a counterexample. This does not stop the statement from compiling! It will however stop any proof of this statement from compiling. Lean carefully distinguishes between the statement of a theorem and the proof of a theorem; humans are very good at referring to both ideas as “a theorem”.
The first question which one has to ask when judging a pdf which comes with some Lean code is: “what is the statement of the theorem in the Lean code, and does this correspond to the actual theorem statement in the pdf?” For a human Lean expert, this is typically (but not always) an easy question to answer. For example any Lean-competent human mathematician would be able to read the two lines of code above and observe that this was a mis-statement of Fermat’s Last Theorem.
Things are, however, not always as easy as this. Currently, because of deficiencies in available libraries, one may have to read many thousands of lines of code just to understand the statement of a formalised theorem. An example of this right now is a PR to DeepMind’s Formal Conjectures repository containing a Lean formalisation of the statement of the Hodge conjecture. At the time of writing, the statement relies on over 10,000 lines of code sitting on top of Mathlib, because Mathlib (which is carefully human-expert-checked and which can be trusted) does not yet have the definitions of things like the cycle class map needed to make the statement. Another example is Axiom’s recent announcement of a formally-verified proof of the classification of finite simple groups. The statement which Axiom’s system proved is here in Tau Ceti, an AI-generated library of Lean code. The file containing the statement imports over 250K lines of Lean code in Tau Ceti (over 900 files). Of these, around 5600 lines of code are crucial because they contain all the relevant definitions (for example, all the definitions of the sporadic simple groups, most of which are still not in Mathlib). Without human checking, one does not really know for sure that this is definitely the correct statement of the classification (and note that I have not yet met any human who claims to have carefully checked that the definitions of the sporadic groups in Tau Ceti are correct). In fact by far the strongest evidence that we have that this statement is correctly formalized is that Axiom’s code proves it!
It is worth noting that of the 290 OpenAI theorems which come with Lean code, around 38 of them have the property that the Lean code does not even state, let alone prove, the main theorem of the paper. And OpenAI never claimed that it did! They just said “here is some Lean code which goes with this paper”. Sometimes the code just states and proves some intermediate results — my impression is that OpenAI decided to go live when some of the formalizations were incomplete, so just dumped what they had. To give a concrete example: paper 194 claims to prove Lech’s multiplicity conjecture in commutative algebra, with no restriction on dimension, residue field or characteristic; this question has been open since 1960. The headline theorem in the corresponding Lean code can be checked to be Corollary 5.4 of the paper — already an impressive achievement, but not the headline result.
Question 2: does the code compile?
Once you’re convinced that you understand the statement of the theorem which the Lean code purports to prove, you (or perhaps one of your friends who has access to a beefy machine, if the code base is huge) has to actually compile the code.
When Anthropic formalized a proof of Fermat’s Last Theorem in Lean, they asked me to take a look at the 13 million lines of code which they had generated. I downloaded it onto my machine, dumped it into a sandbox (because who knows what AI-generated code will do, it can in theory delete all your files) and attempted to compile it; I very quickly ran out of memory. I told Anthropic that I was unable to make any claims about what they had done until I could see the code base compiling, and they gave me temporary access to a machine with 96 cores and 500 gigs of ram. I could then compile the code.
Of course, with a more reasonably-sized codebase it is possible to compile the code on a reasonably-sized machine. For example OpenAI’s resolution of the Navier-Stokes problem is 640K lines of code and compiles fine on my laptop.
It is probably worth stressing again: do not run random Lean code on your local machine unless you sandbox it first. Lean’s mathematics library is safe to run and build upon because this is human-curated and checked by human experts. AI-generated code is not.
Question 3: does the code prove the theorem as stated?
I already talked in Question 1 about the importance of checking the statement of a theorem, so we can be sure that the code is proving the right thing. However, there is an added complication here. Ideally the statement of a theorem will be contained in a file which has very few imports beyond Mathlib, so we know we can trust it. But the proof of the theorem will necessarily import thousands and possibly millions of lines of code which nobody wants to read. How do we know for sure that there is no trick hidden in the millions of lines of proof files which redefines x^n to mean 37, and then proves that a^n + b^n ≠ c^n because the left hand side is 37+37=74 and the right hand side is 37? Or which adds a new axiom to mathematics saying that the theorem is true? Put another way — given a Challenge.lean file with only trusted code imported and the statement of a theorem, and a Solution.lean file with millions of lines of untrusted code imported and the proof of a theorem which looks identical, how do we know for sure that somewhere in the millions of lines of code there is no hack which changes the meaning of the statement, changes the rules from just the axioms of mathematics,  
The one-line answer: lake comparator. You can read more about this answer here. But in short, this tool checks that the theorem stated in a trusted file and the theorem proved via untrusted imports are identical, and that only the axioms of mathematics are used in the proof.
Question 4: does the code exploit a bug in Lean’s official kernel?
This can happen. There was a soundness bug in Lean’s kernel which was fixed four hours after it was discovered, and a subsequent review of Lean’s code base by OpenAI found several more, all of which were fixed before they were announced publicly. There may in theory be more soundness bugs in Lean’s kernel. However, this does not matter.
Why not? Because Lean now has many kernels, created by users, written in many different languages, and at least one of which is formally verified to have no bugs, right down to the assembly level. If you want to make absolutely sure that there is no reward-hacking then again there is a one-line answer: lake comparator --paranoid. A malicious piece of code exploiting an as-yet-undiscovered bug in Lean’s official kernel will not pass this test unless it exploits as-yet-undiscovered bugs in many independent systems all at once. For example this webpage from the Lean kernel arena demonstrates that OpenAI’s resolution of the Navier–Stokes problem is accepted by multiple kernels as well as Lean’s official kernel.
One final remark
Even if the Lean code compiles and passes all these tests, and is thus overwhelmingly likely to be a correct proof of a theorem, this does not mean that any corresponding pdf also contains a correct proof! The Navier–Stokes lost in translation paper demonstrates the opposite in fact, for the Navier-Stokes write-up; whilst all the tests above have been run for the Navier–Stokes work, there are instances where the pdf proof and the Lean proof diverge. In these cases, who knows if the pdf proof is OK! My understanding is that some experts have been using AI to informalise the Lean proof back into English in order to read the argument, rather than ploughing through the slop in the pdf.
Summary/conclusions
“It’s true because it’s checked in Lean” can be made to make sense. But one has to do some work beyond “the Lean code compiles”. Your frontier AI model can do all of this work. But it needs to be done, and (depending on the amount of Lean code in the proof) it may be computationally costly.

articles.title: Big Nuclear isn’t worried about the Democrats stopping data centers
articles.body:
Constellation Energy – America’s largest operator of nuclear power plants – does not share Wall Street’s concerns that the Democrats will slow down data center development. On the company’s third-quarter earnings call last week, CEO Joe Dominguez was, for lack of a better word, unbothered as he addressed the blue wave.
Big Nuclear isn’t worried about the Democrats stopping data centers
They may have a point.
They may have a point.
“I do think we’ve seen a bit of an overreaction in the market to the election results based upon fear that Democrats won’t let data centers get built,” Dominguez said.
Many of the Democrats who seized control of the House and Senate in this month’s midterm elections ran on anti-data-center campaigns, which triggered a historic $2.5 trillion sell-off in AI-adjacent stocks that reached well beyond tech to the energy, construction, and materials sectors.
Up until a few years ago, many of Constellation’s nuclear power plants were in severe financial distress and in danger of shutting down early. But the data center development boom and its enormous demand for electricity have dramatically reversed the nuclear industry’s fate.
Now, Constellation and other companies like it are signing major deals with Big Tech companies to provide power to data centers. Microsoft, for instance, signed a deal with Constellation to fund the revival of a nuclear plant at Three Mile Island in Pennsylvania. (Three Mile Island is the site of what the Nuclear Regulatory Commission refers to as the “most serious accident in US commercial nuclear power plant operating history.”)
Constellation also signed major contracts in the third quarter to provide power to Amazon and Google data centers, Dominguez said.
Nuclear energy has had bipartisan support for years. The US Department of Energy classifies nuclear as a “clean” energy source because the act of operating a nuclear reactor does not directly produce carbon emissions. This makes nuclear an appealing investment to Big Tech companies that have to balance aggressive data center development with the ambitious climate goals they set long before the AI race took off. Still, nuclear energy has its issues. One of the biggest is nuclear waste, which the US government has not figured out how to dispose of at scale.
Big Nuclear and Big Tech also tout these deals as good for the economy and job creation.
“The market scare that people got last week was not lost on Democrats,” Dominguez said on the call. “They do not want to be the reason that the economy takes a nosedive by halting data center development.”
Of course, Constellation’s future is essentially staked on the data center buildout, and Dominguez’s job is to convince investors they have nothing to worry about.
In this instance, however, Dominguez really does seem genuinely unconcerned by the new Democratic majority in the federal government. It could be that he understands that, yes, while the Democrats won the midterms on promises of data center regulation and the blue wave included many new Democratic governors, data centers aren’t necessarily a strictly partisan issue. Some Democrats have opposed harsh measures like moratoriums — though on the flip slide, Constellation may also have to deal with challenges from the other side of the aisle.
In Virginia, some of the state lawmakers who have been the most vocal about data centers are actually Republican. Virginia Sen. Richard Stuart, a conservative Republican, has aggressively pursued data center regulation. Last month, Virginia Gov. Abigail Spanberger, a Democrat, denied Stuart’s request for a special session to address a concerning new report from the Virginia Department of Environmental Quality on the state’s groundwater supply, which has become strained amid rampant data center growth.
For years, companies like Constellation have been sitting on a bunch of old reactors teetering on the edge of extinction because they didn’t have enough customers to keep them afloat.
The fight against data centers so far has been highly fragmented and hyperlocal, but that could change soon. The Trump administration loves data centers, and the federal government is working on wresting some control over data center development away from the states. But even then, Democrats and Republicans at the federal level tend to view data centers as an inevitable part of the future that needs some guardrails rather than out-of-control corporate growth infringing on the average American’s quality of life.
Just look at the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act, which was co-sponsored by two Democrats. The Senate is expected to vote on a passage of a sweeping bill which is being marketed as a way to speed up the permitting process for new power plants and transmission lines and connect new data centers to the grid faster. New Mexico Sen. Martin Heinrich, one of the Democrats backing the bill, has touted its inclusion of provisions designed to protect utility customers from rising rates due to data centers, ensuring Big Tech pays its fair share of costs. Researchers at Columbia University SIPA’s Center on Global Energy Policy called the bill’s protections “mixed,” noting they do not account for wholesale capacity and energy prices, a “principal way” data center electricity demand can lead to higher household bills.
Senate Democrats are sharply divided on the bill, which critics say will fast-track data center projects at the expense of public input and environmental oversight and lead to a massive overbuild of energy projects that Americans will end up paying for.
On Constellation’s earnings call, Dominguez pointed out that Virginia and Illinois, states with Democratic governors already in place before the election, have seen “a great deal of data center development.”
“The bottom line is that Democrats care deeply about economic growth and they care very deeply about the many labor jobs that go with data center construction,” Dominguez said. “With labor such a key constituent for Democrats, it’s hard to imagine that we are going to halt work …There might be some differences and certainly there are going to be some local areas, I think, that are not going to want data centers.”
Of course, Dominguez is speaking to investors here, and he wants to assuage their concerns. He also has a good point. Grassroots efforts to stop local data center development have been successful and have contributed to broader opposition to data center development across the country. But data center developers can also abandon projects and go elsewhere. Until a few years ago, data centers were largely concentrated in Northern Virginia, but with the AI boom, developers have fanned out across the country in search of available power and land. A total of 38 states have welcomed them with open arms and generous tax breaks, per the National Conference of State Legislatures.
Of course, Dominguez is speaking to investors here, and he wants to assuage their concerns.
Thanks to the convoluted way the US electric grid and energy markets work, Constellation’s power plants don’t even need to be located in the same state as their data center customers — the plant supplying the power just needs to be connected to the same region from which the grid is drawing power. The purchase agreement, in that sense, is symbolic: Because the data center needs more electricity than it can draw from the local grid without causing disruptions for everyone else, the data center pays for independent power providers like Constellation to supply the grid with extra electricity.
That’s why data centers and the enormous amount of electricity Big Tech says it needs to power them have been such a boon for the nuclear industry. For years, companies like Constellation have been sitting on a bunch of old reactors teetering on the edge of extinction because they didn’t have enough customers to keep them afloat.
Nuclear lobbyists will tell you that’s because the NRC’s safety regulations are overly restrictive and lead to untenable upfront capital costs that make projects impossible to finance. (This has been an industry talking point since 1979, after the NRC seriously overhauled its safety standards following the partial meltdown at Three Mile Island. That site is now owned by Constellation, which has signed a 20-year deal with Microsoft.)
Both the Biden and Trump administrations have worked to support the development of nuclear power in the US by passing developer tax credits. The Trump administration has gone even further, pushing for a sweeping reform of the NRC that would make it much easier for new reactors to obtain operating licenses.
And the Department of Energy this month approved a $5 billion loan to Constellation, which the company will use to upgrade its existing nuclear fleet. Another nuclear energy company, Vistra, received a $4.2 billion loan.
It’s not totally unlike the Biden administration’s passage of the Civil Nuclear Credit Program in 2022, which planned to loan $6 billion to struggling nuclear companies in the US.
That’s not lost on Dominguez.
“Interestingly, in many respects the election had the Republicans saying a lot of the same things that the Democrats were saying,” Dominguez told investors on the call. “And I believe that the policy solutions are going to be somewhat similar.”

articles.title: The Big Idea: Will Ludwigsen
articles.body:
The Big Idea: Will Ludwigsen
Posted on November 16, 2026 Posted by John Scalzi Leave a Comment
Elder gods and geopolitical quagmires: Are these two great tastes that go great together? Will Ludwigsen mashes up both in A Scout is Loyal — and as this Big Idea shows, the result is intriguing.
WILL LUDWIGSEN:
If you’re wondering (as we all do) how the Vietnam War could possibly have been worse with H.P. Lovecraft’s Deep Ones lurking in the rivers and sea, I’ve written just the book for you.
A Scout is Loyal takes place five years after the events of A Scout is Brave in which Bud Castillo and his Deep One friend Aubrey Marsh thwart a conspiracy to drill into Devil’s Reef in 1963. I wrapped up that Lovecraftian Catcher in the Rye with Bud wistfully gazing out to sea for his lost friend, both of us believing the story was over.
But people had questions, chief among them how discovering a colony of monstrous beings interbreeding with humanity would influence the life of pleasant conformity we’re all expected to embrace. How do you go off to college or get a job without squinting at every bug-eyed pedestrian you pass? Does knowing about a vast cosmic conspiracy make you a Nixon voter or a Humphrey man? Why save for retirement if trans-dimensional beings beyond time can put your brain in a jar?
Lovecraft’s protagonists rarely contend with those long-term implications. They tend to simply faint or gibber when they discover the horrible truth of existence, which appears to be—checking my notes—that humanity’s struggles make no difference to the monstrous beings who truly command the universe.
Which hardly seems a revelation, much less worth going insane over.
At the end of A Scout is Brave, Bud is thirteen years old and now fully aware that the Scout Handbook contains no practical advice for a struggle against overwhelming evil. The best he figures is that we don’t win a single dramatic battle but tiny skirmishes every day, opening literal and figurative doors for others and picking up after ourselves and nudging circumstances toward the good.
My question for the sequel became, “What the hell does a Boy Scout like that do in Vietnam?”
A lunatic—say, me—could make a case that the Vietnam War may well have been our most Boy Scout-y conflict, driven by total arrogant confidence that we were rescuing “helpless” people to impose our values on them. We rationalized our baser motives with the spangled bunting of altruism because we were the Good Guys walking little old Vietnamese ladies across the street to freedom.
It also had lots of hiking and camping.
What Bud discovers when he gets to Vietnam in A Scout is Loyal isn’t a lack of idealism but a glut of it. He’s surrounded by people who are proud of the extremes they’ll take to prove their vision for reality is the right one. How can you talk someone off a ledge when they think they’re virtuous for being there?
That’s where Lovecraft, scouting, and Vietnam converge: the myopia of utter conviction. Lovecraft’s (human) bad guys were true believers with the advantage of certainty, and his good guys were skeptics with the “disadvantage” of an open mind. Those strike me as the real-world bad guys and good guys in Vietnam, too, confident zealots versus the few still asking questions of themselves.
In A Scout is Loyal, Bud’s worst errors of perception and action occur when he feels the most certain, the most electrified with righteous purpose. His struggle is to let new information change his mind, and in that way, he has a lot in common with Nixon and McNamara and Kissinger, and honestly the rest of us.
Sometimes the smoothest road to being wrong is being sure.
I didn’t write A Scout is Loyal as a “message” book—every great error of my life came from thinking I knew an absolute truth—but as an experiential one. I wondered how someone like Bud (or like me) would react to that impossible situation where being right didn’t seem to matter as much as believing you were. I ran the scenario and reported what happened.
The closest my book gets to a “Big Idea” is that Big Ideas are liars. They’re the smoothed edges and blunted corners of reality, the models and rules of thumb that make us miss the details that hurt other people.
Lovecraft’s big idea was that we don’t matter in a terrifying cosmos. Mine, if these books have one, is that we only have to matter to each other.
A Scout is Loyal: Amazon|Barnes & Noble|Bookshop|Lethe Press
Author socials: Website|Bluesky

articles.title: Corporations Are Using Trump's Tariff Refunds On Bonuses Rather Than Reimbursing
articles.body:
Corporations Are Using Trump's Tariff Refunds On Bonuses Rather Than Reimbursing (propublica.org) 78
			
		 	
				An anonymous reader quotes a report from ProPublica: When Stanley Black & Decker, one of the world's largest tool companies, got hit with President Donald Trump's tariffs last year, the firm made clear that it would be sharing the pain with its customers. The Connecticut-based company raised prices again and again, moves its executives said were necessary because of the new fees on imports. Now, after the Supreme Court struck down Trump's most sweeping tariffs earlier this year, the company is getting at least $298 million refunded. Instead of sharing that bounty with its customers, however, the firm has chosen different recipients: Its own leaders. The company is one of at least nine that have disclosed that they are using their refunds not to pay back the cash-strapped consumers who generally covered much of the tariff costs through higher prices, but to give bonuses, according to a ProPublica analysis of thousands of securities filings and earnings calls for publicly traded companies.
Other recognizable companies include the owners of discount department stores TJ Maxx and Marshalls and the golf equipment brand Titleist. Dozens of other firms have said little about how they plan to use the money other than to characterize the windfall as the kind of earnings they use to determine executive bonuses. The Trump administration has not publicly detailed which companies are getting the roughly $170 billion in refunds or how much they've asked for, and it has denied ProPublica's requests for this information. But reporters found some of these details while reviewing the disclosures of thousands of publicly traded companies.
Some have described vague plans to pay the money forward by, for example, "returning tariff refunds to our members through pricing," though they generally don't say whether that involves price cuts or limiting future increases. Others are paying back businesses they sold products to because they had itemized receipts that detailed the tariff markups. But consumers hoping for refunds appear to be largely out of luck. With the help of artificial intelligence, ProPublica identified companies that said they planned to refund customers with their tariff windfalls. Almost all of them deal with other businesses, not consumers. "Executive bonuses are probably the least just way to use this money because it wasn't anything the executives did that they should be rewarded for. It was a government mistake that resulted in a refund," said Gregory Germain, a corporate law professor at Syracuse University. "It really explains why it's so important for the government, when they're doing something like this, to think it through to make sure consumers don't pay extra money and not get it back."

articles.title: How Billions in Safe Insurance Money Is Being Bet on A.I. Debt
articles.body:
Supported by
How Billions in Safe Insurance Money Is Being Bet on A.I. Debt
Insurance companies are investing billions of their customers’ money into A.I. deals as analysts warn of mounting risks.
When Elon Musk needed help financing a large purchase of artificial intelligence chips earlier this year, Wall Street offered an elegant solution.
Mr. Musk and his team of advisers created a financial entity that would borrow billions to buy the chips and then lease them back to xAI, his artificial intelligence effort. This way, xAI wasn’t technically the borrower, which helped make its official debt load look smaller to investors.
To help fund this complicated arrangement, $2.4 billion of the debt was sold to an insurance company called Athene, which manages life insurance policies and annuities for retirees, according to a Moody’s Ratings report.
The deal was part of an increasingly popular playbook: tapping insurance companies, which are historically among the most cautious investors, to make loans to tech titans like Mr. Musk and further fuel the A.I. boom.
The amount of A.I. debt being held by insurance companies has soared this year. U.S. life insurers, including some of the largest like Athene and Corebridge Financial, held $85.2 billion in A.I. debt as of June 30, up 24 percent from six months prior, according to Moody’s.
While this accounts for just 2.1 percent of life insurers’ total debt, their exposure is expected to grow quickly. Life insurers could hold up to $185 billion of A.I. investments by the end of next year, according to Moody’s.

articles.title: Doing Show HN generates a ton of automated email pitches
articles.body:
Show HN -> a ton of automated email pitches
I posted Airdash on Show HN last week. Over the next four days, 17 services wrote to the Airdash inbox to sell me something, and nearly all of them were written by software that read my HN title and nothing else.
Let's go through it.
Seven of the 17 are launch boards and directories: AI tool lists, "Product of the Week" battles, a 3D city map of SaaS products. The hook is usually a dofollow backlink, the price somewhere between free and $49. The other ten sell security scans, competitor reports, agent testing, demo videos, Reddit promotion, newsletter sponsorships, distribution to other people's coding agents, and one wants an affiliate deal.

One directory pasted my whole Show HN title in as the product name, so it would love to feature "I built SQLite databases for your agents with an Airtable view for you."
"No follow-ups, promise." "This is the only email you'll get about it." "Not a mailing list, just a one-time note." One of them then sent me the same pitch three times.

I run [Service] and have a labelled sponsor seat open. First month free, then $29/mo, locked 6 months, month to month.

[link]
Not relevant? Just reply "no" and I won't email again.
[Name]
