Nvidia’s board is reportedly ‘not considering’ hiring Jensen Huang back
articles.body:
Nvidia’s board of directors “isn’t considering” having Jensen Huang return as CEO, according to a report from CNBC. A source tells the outlet the board “is focused on an investigation into Huang, and is not in discussions to bring him back.”
Nvidia’s board is reportedly ‘not considering’ hiring Jensen Huang back
Nvidia’s board of directors is still focused on an investigation into Huang, CNBC reports.
Since Huang’s resignation last week, tech executives, along with current and former Nvidia employees, have called for his reinstatement. An online petition to bring Huang back as CEO has amassed more than 180,000 signatures, including from major figures like Epic Games CEO Tim Sweeney, SpaceX CEO Elon Musk, and Replit CEO Amjad Masad.
President Donald Trump said on Monday that it “certainly isn’t a bad idea” for Huang to return to Nvidia. A report from the Financial Times also suggests that Huang floated the idea of returning as CEO with some of his colleagues.
Nvidia appointed its chief financial officer, Colette Kress, as interim CEO. The company has also hired Wachtell Lipton to investigate Huang’s conduct.

articles.title: United Airlines system outage disrupts departures just days after the big ground stop
articles.body:
Less than a week after an issue with air traffic control communications and radar caused the FAA to halt takeoffs nationwide, United Airlines departing flights are being disrupted by an outage. At 6:13PM ET, United said the problem has been fixed:
United Airlines system outage disrupts departures just days after the big ground stop
Is everything down right now?
Is everything down right now?
Earlier today we experienced a technology-related issue that impacted some departing flights. The issue has been resolved. Please check the latest status of your flight at united.com or the United app.
The outage is also coming after last week’s global Microsoft Outlook shutdown, and the great-bank-outage-that-wasn’t earlier Monday afternoon. According to posts on social media, a number of people onboard the planes have heard from their pilots that a systemwide IT outage for United has caused problems with a weight and balance calculator that has stopped them from getting clearance to take off.
United tweeted earlier that “We are troubleshooting a technology issue affecting departing flights. There is no impact on flights in progress, or on United Express flights.”
Update, November 16th: Added note that United says the problem has been resolved.

articles.title: US data centers now burn more electricity than a midsized country
articles.body:
Fossil fuels are still the biggest source of electricity for hyperscale data centers in the US, a new paper published in the journal Nature Sustainability shows. They likely burn through more electricity collectively than many countries do, resulting in a serious amount of greenhouse gas emissions.
US data centers now burn more electricity than a midsized country
The latest numbers are in on how much energy hyperscale data centers use and the carbon pollution they create.
The study homes in on hyperscale facilities — the massive structures spanning millions of square feet that developers are racing to build in large part to support generative AI. Researchers say the findings show that there’s a lot of work left to do to cut down pollution stemming from AI’s reliance on fossil fuels.
“We tend to discuss AI’s environmental footprint as though it were some fixed property of the technology, when in reality the same computing infrastructure can have dramatically different consequences depending on the electricity system supporting it,” Gianluca Guidi, lead author of the new study and a postdoctoral fellow in the Department of Biostatistics at Harvard T.H. Chan School of Public Health, says in an email to The Verge. “I actually find that encouraging, because it means these impacts aren’t inevitable. We have choices about where we build and how we power this infrastructure.”
“The same computing infrastructure can have dramatically different consequences depending on the electricity system supporting it.”
Guidi and his team used satellite imagery to identify 403 hyperscale data centers in the US, estimating each facility’s power consumption based on its electrical capacity. Using data from the Environmental Protection Agency, they approximated how much carbon pollution each data center would have produced if connected to the local power grid between May 2024 and April 2025.
Altogether, the 403 hyperscale facilities likely consumed around 82 terawatt-hours of electricity that year, about 1.8 percent of all US electricity consumption. That’s even more than the amount of electricity that about 148 nations — a majority of the countries in the world including Austria, Israel, and Venezuela but excluding the largest economies including the US and China — individually burn through each year, according to John Sterman, director of the MIT System Dynamics group and MIT Sloan Sustainability Initiative.
Electricity demand from these data centers produced 25.7 million metric tons of CO2 emissions, comparable to the annual carbon footprint of Denmark, according to the research paper. Sterman says that exceeds the total carbon emissions of about 113 nations. That’s because about 54 percent of the electricity the hyperscale facilities consumed likely came from gas and coal.
Sterman, who was not involved in the research with Guidi, disclosed that he used the help of Claude to compare the paper’s findings to electricity use and emissions of countries. “I think AI can be extraordinarily helpful,” Sterman says. “But we’ve got to figure out a way to limit the harms … Especially because those impacts are irreversible. Once you allow these data centers to emit the CO2, you can never undo that.”
Sterman says policymakers should require data center operators to bring new clean energy online. The study doesn’t account for local air pollution that can result from new gas infrastructure that’s being built to meet data center demand, or gas turbines that some AI companies have installed at their facilities to power themselves without connecting to the grid. And while hyperscale data centers encompass more than just AI-related computing, they also make up just a fraction of the thousands of data centers in the US — with more cropping up each year.
The study showed how big a difference the local electricity mix makes when it comes to the environmental impact of AI and data centers. Generating electricity in heavily coal-reliant Wyoming led to roughly seven times more carbon emissions per kilowatt-hour than in hydropower-rich Oregon. “Two data centers consuming exactly the same amount of electricity can have dramatically different carbon footprints simply because of where they’re located,” Guidi writes.
Fengqi You, a professor in energy systems engineering at Cornell University who was also not involved in the study, says the results highlight the problem of “long-term carbon lock-in.” “Power plants and supporting infrastructure built to meet rapidly growing data center demand may operate for decades. Decisions made today could therefore shape emissions well into the future,” You says in an email to The Verge.
Both You and Guidi also pointed out how problematic it is that researchers have to go through such great lengths to estimate energy consumption because data center operators won’t disclose that information. To that end, Guidi and his colleagues are using their research to build a website to track the environmental impact of individual data centers. A bipartisan bill making its way through Congress could also mandate greater disclosures nationally on data centers’ electricity use.
“Communities and policymakers need reliable, independent data on what these facilities mean for our air, health, and the climate. This study is an important step.” Gina McCarthy, former White House national climate advisor and EPA administrator, said in a statement shared by the research authors.

articles.title: Robert Pattinson Is Officially James Bond
articles.body:
It’s Pattinson, Robert Pattinson.
The “Batman” and “Odyssey” star has officially been cast as the next James Bond, ending months of rabid speculation about which young actor Amazon MGM and director Denis Villeneuve would hand the keys to the Aston Martin.
“James Bond is one of the most legendary characters in cinema, and to be entrusted with 007 is the honor of a lifetime,” Pattinson said in a statement. “I’m deeply grateful to Denis, Amy, David, Tanya and everyone at Amazon MGM Studios for their belief in me. To say this role is a dream come true is an understatement. I couldn’t be more excited about this partnership and the work ahead with this fantastic team.”
Added Villeneuve, who recently directed Pattinson in the upcoming “Dune: Part Three”: “Before anything else, I want to express my deep gratitude to the remarkable actors who joined us on this journey. We were surrounded by extraordinary talent, but there can only be one 007. I am overjoyed to welcome Robert Pattinson as our new James Bond. He has the timeless soul of 007 and brings a spirit that is completely new. I cannot wait to begin.”
Amy Pascal, a key architect of the “Spider-Man” franchise, and David Heyman, behind the “Harry Potter” series, are producing the new Bond film, with Tanya Lapointe executive producing. Steven Knight is writing the screenplay.
Pattinson picks up the 007 mantle after Daniel Craig’s five-movie run as the womanizing super spy, which began in 2006 with “Casino Royale.” Craig’s final turn was in 2021’s “No Time to Die,” which ends with Bond sacrificing himself to save the world from a secret global terrorist organization. “No Time to Die” was also the last film in the series released before longtime producers Michael G. Wilson and Barbara Broccoli sold creative control of the franchise to Amazon MGM for $20 million.
Predictions about who would be the next James Bond had taken over media and the industry in the last month, and a shortlist of British actors took turns as the presumed favorite. Jacob Elordi was pegged for the role in the earliest days of swirling rumors, but reports since surfaced that the “Euphoria” star didn’t even screen test for the part. Jack Lowden seemed like another safe bet. In early September, his “Slow Horses” co-star Gary Oldman claimed Bond was already picked and cheekily added that his “fingers are crossed” for Lowden. However, Lowden’s run at the character was largely overshadowed by Callum Turner, who seemed like a sure pick until news of Pattinson and Nicholas Hoult’s auditions was revealed. At that point, it became anyone’s guess who would come out on top until Pattinson was ultimately chosen. Other actors in the mix included Josh O’Connor, Tom Francis, Aaron Taylor-Johnson, Harris Dickinson and even Harry Styles.
It’s not hard to see from Amazon MGM’s perspective why Pattinson was the obvious choice. He is, almost unquestionably, 2026’s most in-demand movie star and has the box office record to show for it. With help from Zendaya, Pattinson drove A24’s “The Drama,” an intimate yet squirmy original dramedy, to $134 million worldwide from a budget of $28 million. “Primetime,” in which Pattinson starred as “To Catch a Predator” host Chris Hansen, likewise hit big with $61 million globally against a slim $18 million budget. Pattinson also starred as the sniveling Antinous in “The Odyssey,” which did $1.8 billion, and is set to star in “Dune: Part Three” in December, which is sure to pull in the big bucks. (It’s very possible Pattinson earned the part after impressing Villeneuve on Arrakis).
Pattinson also has the big IP experience needed to lead a franchise like James Bond. In 2022, Pattinson debuted as the titular Caped Crusader in Matt Reeves’ “The Batman.” He is set to revisit Gotham for the sequel in 2028. Those doubting Pattinson would land 007 often pointed to his obligations to Bruce Wayne as a reason why he could never take on Bond. However, after several production delays with “The Batman Part II,” it seems Pattinson is ready for a new longterm relationship with another familiar big-screen icon.
“James Bond is one of the most beloved, inspiring, iconic and yet enigmatic characters in literature and movies,” said producers Pascal and Heyman. “The legacy of this character is in great hands with Robert Pattinson. His fearlessness as an actor, his self-deprecating wit and his ability to continually reinvent himself make him the perfect Bond for our times.”

articles.title: Grazing sheep in fields with solar arrays
articles.body:
Sheep grazing in solar fields offers farmers economic, ecological gains
By Krisy Gashler
Two new research papers shed light on the growing practice of grazing sheep in fields with solar arrays. One demonstrates that, in the right numbers, sheep grazing increases populations of beneficial insects like bees and lady beetles compared to mowing around solar panels. The other research describes a decision-making support tool to help farmers profitably grow their solar grazing herds.
A team from the College of Agriculture and Life Sciences (CALS) found that when two sheep per hectare graze around solar arrays, the abundance of wild bees, honey bees and lady beetles jumped by 38%, compared to a control plot that was mowed. The increase was driven primarily by an 83% increase in honey bees alone, according to the team’s findings in “Low solar-grazing densities support beneficial insects in agrivoltaic systems,” published Oct. 7 in Environmental Research Letters.
“Sheep grazing and beneficial insect habitat are two prominent conversation topics around solar development right now,” said Leana Zoller, the paper’s first author and a postdoctoral associate in natural resources in the Cornell CALS Ashley School of Global Development and the Environment. “But what’s been missing is research that treats them as parts of the same system. When we talk about sustainable solar development, integrating these discussions into a single framework is really helpful to farmers and community decision makers.”
For three years, Zoller and a team of entomologists, ecologists and animal and plant scientists tested various stocking rates – how many sheep per hectare are allowed to graze a certain plot of land – using Cornell’s teaching sheep grazing at the university-owned Cascadilla Community Solar Farm in Dryden, New York. At four sheep per hectare, they found beneficial insect abundance was similar to the mowed control site, while vegetation management effectiveness was greater than at two sheep per hectare. At eight sheep per hectare, vegetation management was maximized and sheep flock health remained high, but honey bee abundance dropped by 45%.
“We zeroed in on stocking rates because that’s a concrete number that sheep farmers understand and work with every day, and we want this research to be useful,” said Steve Grodsky, paper senior author and assistant professor of natural resources in the Ashley School. “With solar grazing, people, energy, agricultural animals, plants and insects are all part of this ecosystem. We’re trying to understand the connections between those pieces so that when solar developers, municipalities looking at solar development, or farmers are faced with a decision, they can have scientific information about potential trade-offs and synergies.”
Grodsky is also assistant unit leader of the U.S. Geological Survey New York Cooperative Fish and Wildlife Research Unit. Additional co-authors are sheep farmer and solar grazing consultant Nikola Kochendoerfer, Ph.D. ’20; Antonio DiTommaso, professor in the School of Integrative Plant Science; John Losey, professor of entomology; Scott McArt, Ph.D. ’12, associate professor of entomology; Paige Muñiz, formerly a technician in McArt’s lab; and Todd Ugine, Ph.D. ’04, research associate in Losey’s lab, all in CALS. Sarah Carson, director of Cornell’s Campus Sustainability Office, was key in coordinating site access between researchers and the solar company that manages the Cascadilla solar farm.
Another Cornell research team, from the Cornell SC Johnson College of Business, has developed a tool that helps farmers whose sheep graze in solar arrays to make better decisions about their operation. The team described the tool in “Flock Management for Solar Grazing,” which published Sept. 28 in Manufacturing & Service Operations Management.
After a chance encounter with Caleb Scott, Ithaca-based sheep farmer and founder of United Agrivoltaics, Vincent Slaugh, assistant professor at the Cornell Peter and Stephanie Nolan School of Hotel Administration and first author of the paper, began thinking through the economics and logistics of solar grazing. He recruited Linwei Xin, associate professor of operations research and information engineering, and Shane Henderson, Charles W. Lake, Jr. Professor in Productivity, both in the Cornell Duffield College of Engineering, to work on the topic.
Together, they developed a spreadsheet-based model that helps sheep farmers to optimize procurement and sales decisions, based on factors like target flock size, costs, anticipated revenues, and expected vegetation in particular solar sites; if a farmer doesn’t have enough sheep to keep the grass down, they’ll have to cut it some other way. It also helps solar developers understand growers’ needs and develop contracts that are more profitable and sustainable for all parties long-term. United Agrivoltaics has already incorporated the tool into its onboarding process.
Slaugh sees opportunity for U.S. shepherds to grow their operations – especially with solar contracts offering a steady source of income and animal feed. Current domestic sheep production for meat and wool doesn’t come close to meeting domestic demand; about half of all lamb and mutton consumed in the U.S. is imported, primarily from New Zealand and Australia.
“If we grow the sheep industry, will the American diet eventually include more lamb? Could that be a side effect of the solar energy revolution? I think the answer is very likely yes,” Slaugh said. “And then when that happens, we’d expect processors and supporting industries to come back, for banks to be willing to give more loans, and for supply chains to follow. All of that grows the economy, and rural economies in particular.”
Kochendoerfer, who grazes 700 ewes on solar installations in New York and Vermont, said that economy is already growing.
“I work with a lot of farms that are now scaling up because of solar,” Kochendoerfer said. “There is a new wave of sheep farmers who are capitalizing on this access to good land. With solar grazing, you get paid to graze as opposed to having to pay to graze. That leads to sustainable, meaningful economic income that these farmers can use to expand, build a barn, buy equipment or hire someone. It’s enabling a lot of folks to build sound, viable agricultural businesses.”
Funding for these research projects came from the Cornell Atkinson Center for Sustainability, the National Institute for Food and Agriculture and the National Science Foundation.
Krisy Gashler is a writer for the College of Agriculture and Life Sciences.

It’s enabling a lot of folks to build sound, viable agricultural businesses.”

articles.title: It's always DNS, so why are we running our own?
articles.body:
This will be a rollercoaster story on how we ended up replacing Route53 and running our own authoritative DNS server.
Before our lives changed
At some point, we decided we should be able to provide unlimited basins to our clients. Basins are a core namespace construct on S2 and act as top-level containers for streams (already unlimited in number). We found that customers were hacking around our not-so-arbitrary limit of 100 basins per account. That’s not a cool experience.
For the purposes of this story, what is important is that each basin created by a customer becomes its own subdomain: my-basin.b.s2.dev (not different from the way buckets work on AWS S3). The DNS entry associated with each basin is a CNAME, which routes clients to the correct cell in our architecture. To support unlimited basins, we'd therefore need to support unlimited DNS records.
These records would need strong consistency too. When a basin is created, its address should be instantly resolvable, otherwise clients would be waiting around for a cached NXDOMAIN to expire.
My pulse went through the roof at the thought of running our own DNS server, yikes!
Hooking on existing systems
My research phase started with hope. Hope that our existing DNS setup with AWS Route53 would work with these new requirements. I really really did not want us to build and run our own DNS server.
Route53 is an awesome system and can, it appears, support an unlimited number of records. But, there's a fatal limitation: their API rate limits at a max of about 5 UPSERTs per second (AWS throttling docs have recently changed, the limits may be higher now).
This was something we discovered the hard way, actually. I did read the docs but the API limits didn’t raise any concerns. It became obvious when a nefarious actor rapidly created 10s of thousands of basins, saturating our entire quota of Route53 records. This generated a backlog of work that required a few hours to process, during which our normal DNS updates were stuck, with processes trying to delete records while others tried to add new records. It did make for a great post-incident review though. This was when we started enforcing the 100 basins per account limit.
We looked at the option of batching, but that would break our goal of making entries instantly available. And even with batching, the setup did not feel “unlimited”; it would still be possible for legitimate use of the system to hit the rate limit.
Other managed DNS providers we looked at (GCP Cloud DNS, Cloudflare, Azure DNS) have similar limitations: if you update/insert/upsert records using the provider API, there’s a heavy limiting component.
No way around it, a custom authoritative DNS server had to be built (double yikes!)
The new DNS system
The technical requirements were pretty straightforward: given any DNS request that comes in, we need to query an up-to-date zone map, which should be able to hold unlimited records, and send a corresponding response back to the client.
To avoid syncing to a separate system and having yet another moving piece, the DNS records would come directly from our existing basin database. A live SELECT would consistently “resolve” the required mapping in the DNS request. In other words, we wanted DNS to simply become a new caller of our existing, strongly consistent account database.
Our account database lives in Google’s Cloud Spanner where performance was expected to fare well (given enough money that is).
Next came the core functionality.
We went back and forth between building on a library or writing a CoreDNS module. A library ended up feeling like the most flexible path, which would allow us to build something very specific to our use case. We are a Rust shop, but we decided to go with Go for this project, mostly because the Spanner tooling (and the GCP ecosystem) is comparatively more mature. We quickly settled on the miekg/dns library due to its excellent doc quality and the many RFCs under its belt.
We needed to be able to support authoritative DNS queries for several types of records: A, AAAA, NS, CNAME, SOA. Since we were using a library we had to build the responses ourselves. Our correctness testing focused on these, and consisted of unit tests, RFC compliance testing using Ferret (which we discovered in this great paper: SCALE: Automatically Finding RFC Compliance Bugs in DNS Nameservers) and a post-deploy smoke test with live data.
S2 uses wildcard certificates for the basin zone and they need ACME DNS-01 challenges to work. We decided not to serve the DNS challenge from our server and offloaded it to a separate Route53 zone using CNAME delegation, to avoid tweaking our cert renewal systems as well as serving dynamic TXT records.
We then went through a few planning sessions with a popular AI system. The design was simple enough, things made a lot of sense (even for me), except that the recommendations constantly included various extra features: coalescing, negative caching, throttling, rate limiting, DNS cookies, etc. Expected, for a system that would sit live on the open scary internet; however, it was a lot of suggested protection.
The more we pulled on this thread ... the scarier it got. There are many types of attacks that can happen at the DNS level, scary things I knew of and things I never heard of.
NXDOMAIN attack is the one that made us the most afraid. Every random non-existent DNS query would be a fresh database lookup. We tried building in-app defenses for NXDOMAIN however, it is, in my opinion, the worst DDoS attack and nothing can really stop it. Not cool.
The case for a DNS Firewall
Long story short, the possible attacks on DNS infrastructure scared me more than I would like to admit. We went looking for a DNS firewall solution. We were sure there must be something like a reverse proxy setup for DNS serving. Either this is a niche setup or it’s a very dangerous world, but for our requirements of unlimited records and DNS reverse-proxy firewall type, we found only two companies: Cloudflare and Akamai. Both giants in their own rights, both with similar offerings (it’s the kind that has no public pricing).
A few POCs later, we ended up picking Cloudflares DNS Firewall solution. Our DNS server origins were configured to only allow traffic from Cloudflare’s known IPs, a pretty standard reverse-CF setup (Cloudflare in front and nobody else gets to the origin, otherwise what’s the point). With this missing piece, we were now at our final design and ready to roll the new system into production.
As an authoritative DNS server, we have to reply to SOA and NS queries, and they point to nameserver IPs. We took extra care to ensure the IPs returned are always the Cloudflare IPs and not the load balancer ones, which included a ns-leak-test that ensures the origin IPs don't leak as part of some regression change.
Final architecture
For the final architecture and HA (yes, failures will always happen), we run the DNS server on two separate GKE clusters (in separate regions, choosing the closest possible to Spanner), each with multiple replicas behind a TCP and UDP load balancer.
Observability and training everyone on the new system were another key component of the rollout. While I don’t think anyone gives Route53 a second thought and I don’t think anyone monitors it separately (managed services are someone else’s pager after all), we had to create alerts and runbooks with late-night processes to recover from failures.
There is one funny part to this setup: explaining the full delegation chain. The main domain is managed by Cloudflare in a regular zone. Then it delegates the basin subdomain to Cloudflare, but not a zone, to a service (DNS Firewall). That service then connects to GKE. And there’s another zone in Route53 for the certs (good luck understanding that, Codex).
This isn’t even its final form, the internal TODO includes tuning DNS caching and how to properly optimize between clients/DNS Firewall/DNS app (no amount of AI can solve that), future DNSSEC extensions and many more. It is an unknown system when it comes to failures we don’t see (or the way I like to think about this, how do you know things fail when they look fine).
For now, things have been stable. Looking at stats for the past few weeks, live traffic looks good, the commit history for the past few weeks is mostly CVE fixes, dependency bumps and cost savings. Our customers now create thousands of basins, and they are instantly available for streaming.
I think we’re now in a place where we can blame DNS in one of our post-incident reviews.

articles.title: How to Break into Security, Ptacek Edition (2012)
articles.body:
At least once a month, sometimes more, readers write in to ask how they can break into the field of computer security. Some of the emails are from people in jobs that have nothing to do with security, but who are fascinated enough by the field to contemplate a career change. Others are already in an information technology position but are itching to segue into security. I always respond with my own set of stock answers, but each time I do this, I can’t help but feel my advice is incomplete, or at least not terribly well-rounded.
I decided to ask some of the brightest minds in the security industry today what advice they’d give. Almost everyone I asked said they, too, frequently get asked the very same question, but each had surprisingly different takes on the subject. Today is the first installment in a series of responses to this question. When the last of the advice columns have run, I’ll create an archive of them all that will be anchored somewhere prominently on the home page. That way, the next time someone asks how they can break into security, I’ll have more to offer than just my admittedly narrow perspectives on the matter.
Last month, I interviewed Thomas Ptacek, founder of Matasano Security, about how companies could beef up password security in the wake of a week full of news about password leaks at LinkedIn and other online businesses. Ptacek’s provocative advice generated such a huge amount of reader interest and further discussion that I thought it made sense to begin this series with his thoughts:
Ptacek: “Information security is one of the most interesting, challenging, and, if you do it carefully, rewarding fields in the technology industry. It’s one of the few technology jobs where the most fun roles are well compensated. If you grew up dreaming of developing games, the laws of supply and demand teach a harsh lesson early in your career: game development jobs are often tedious and usually pay badly. But if you watched “Sneakers” and ideated a life spent breaking or defending software, great news: infosec can be more fun in real life, and it’s fairly lucrative.
I’m a software developer. I try to look at security through the lens of computer science. To me, the most attractive thing about the field is the opportunity it provides to work with lots of different concepts at lots of different levels. Computer security might be the best way to work professionally with compiler theory, or to spend time understanding computer microarchitecture, or to apply advanced mathematics.
Other people get involved in security for different reasons, and those reasons are probably equally valid. Some people really like the “good guys / bad guys” narrative that comes with security. Some people see security as an opportunity to save the world. Other people are drawn to the competitive nature of the field: at the higher levels, it really is a cat-and-mouse game. It also comes closer to meritocracy than most of technology: you can either break in or you can’t; your defenses either work or they don’t.
But for me, it’s just one of the best development jobs you can get, and with that in mind, here’s my advice for people interested in pursuing a career in it.
First: I want you to learn how to program. Clearly, you can get through college and get a good-paying steady job without ever learning to love programming. But no one factor gives you as much control over your career, as much of an ability to write your own ticket, as the ability to solve problems using programming languages. A lot of very smart technology professionals have concluded that they just don’t enjoy writing software. Those people should reconsider. Try different languages, or different application domains, but find a way to make programming stick in your head.
Second: the best jobs in our field are in application security. You can get good steady work designing firewall deployments, setting up desktop agents, or responding to incidents. But all those roles are fundamentally reacting to what’s happening in appsec. The next generation of security products — along with the org charts of security teams at the savviest companies — are being designed now, by accident, by application security practitioners.
Appsec roles are roles that involve attacking software or devising fixes and countermeasures for those attacks. Two good ways to “come up” in appsec: become a penetration tester, or contribute to (or start) a secure software development practice in your company.
A good way to move into penetration testing: grab some industry standard tools and use an Amazon EC2 account to set up a “shooting range” to attack. Some of the best-known tools are available for free: the Nessus scanner, for instance, while not an application security tool, is free and can land you a network penetration testing role that you can use as a springboard to breaking applications.
When people reach out to Matasano asking how to get a foot in the door attacking software, we have a few simple steps to offer:
0. Learn to love programming in at least one language. The C Programming Language has the most cachet in application security, but for this step-by-step list, Java or Python or Ruby will do fine.
1. Grab a copy of The Web Application Hacker’s Handbook.
2. Go to the “previous releases” archive at WordPress.org and grab very old versions of WordPress; install them at EC2.
3. Download OWASP WebScarab or Burp Suite Free Edition, both of which are free, and use them to find bugs in ancient WordPress.
If you’re already in an IT role, and want to come up on the defensive side of appsec, try to position yourself near custom software development. Most large firms build “line of business” applications. As a rule, building “line of business” isn’t particularly fun. But defending those apps can be; sometimes, the most boring applications turn out to be surprisingly sensitive.
And the good news for doing appsec in BigCo’s: most companies have very immature security programs. If you can get a role in QA, or in what the cool kids are calling “DevOps”, you can end up with a lot of influence in security. At Matasano, we’ve watched lots of ops people successfully transition to appsec and senior security management just by instituting basic security testing processes on their company’s software.
To me, the whole field boils down to studying, understanding, and manipulating technology. Like most software security practices, we’ve gotten our hands dirty with a fascinating cross-section of the whole technology industry. We’ve written attack tools that target the control registers of device chipsets, we’ve done custom RF work, we’ve written low-level debuggers for different CPU architectures, and we’ve seen and beaten up on products built in almost every programming language and every platform you can imagine. If crawling through the ventilation ducts of the world’s most important technology is something you think might make you tick like we do… well, appsec! Learn to code. Spend a couple days Starbucks money on an EC2 account and deploy some broken apps to break. Find opportunities to practice in your job.
And, uh, come talk to us? People like you are hard to find!”

articles.title: California sues OpenAI over rogue AI hacking incidents
articles.body:
California is suing OpenAI after its AI agents broke out of their testing environment and hacked other companies, including Hugging Face. In a lawsuit filed Monday, Attorney General Rob Bonta accuses OpenAI of violating consumer safety law by knowingly developing a “dangerous product without proper oversight,” as reported earlier by Reuters.
California sues OpenAI over rogue AI hacking incidents
OpenAI lost control of its AI agents more than 80 times during testing, California’s AG claims.
The lawsuit claims the cyberattack on Hugging Face “was the predictable result of an internal culture at OpenAI that prioritizes growth and rapid model development over safety and accountability.” It alleges that OpenAI recently told the attorney general’s office that it “lost control” of its AI agents more than 80 times during testing.
After revealing the rogue AI attack on Hugging Face in July, news of several other similar incidents emerged, including attacks on an Australian government website, a German wiki site, and the software package manager RubyGems. OpenAI’s agents also tried to “bruteforce” a United Nations website.
“OpenAI’s actions escalated real-world cybersecurity risks, threatening the safety, health, and well-being of society,” Bonta says in the press release. “The company knowingly tested a dangerous product without proper oversight or safety procedures and misled the public about it — this disregard for public safety violated California law.”
OpenAI released its new cybersecurity AI model earlier this month, saying that it’s less likely to go rogue and attack other platforms. It’s also giving safety evaluators at Apollo Research access to its AI systems as part of a pilot program that monitors models for misalignment.
“Since the Hugging Face incident, we’ve undertaken an extensive and transparent effort to understand and address misaligned model activity,” OpenAI spokesperson Drew Pusateri says in an emailed statement to The Verge. “This lawsuit appears to single out OpenAI over a challenge that’s been identified by every major AI lab. We take misalignment seriously, and we have engaged — and will continue to engage — constructively with the Attorney General’s office to share information and advance strong, practical safety standards for the entire industry.”

articles.title: Sony’s PlayStation 5 accessories are cheaper ahead of Black Friday
articles.body:
Several retailers are offering discounts on PlayStation 5 games, including deep price cuts on recent console-exclusive hits like Marvel’s Wolverine, Ghost of Yotei, Saros, and hundreds more. We’ll cover a bunch of those in the coming days, but this post is focused on the great hardware discounts that are happening, including $20 off the stellar DualSense wireless controller and its many color schemes, as well as $30 off the customizable DualSense Edge. The big sale also extends to headsets, console covers, and even Sony’s 27-inch monitor that has a hook to charge your controller.
Sony’s PlayStation 5 accessories are cheaper ahead of Black Friday
Plenty of deals to glam up your PS5, whether you want a new console cover, a headset, or a unique DualSense color.
Sitting out from the discounts, at least for now, are new PlayStation 5 consoles. It’s not impossible that a deal will surface later this month, though it’s more unlikely to happen than in past years for a couple of reasons. For one, console deals are exceedingly rare due to the rise in costs for the consoles associated with RAMageddon. articles.title: Launch HN: Axonnic (YC F26) – Sleeves that track fingers and estimate force
articles.body:
Hi HN! We’re Arsh and Max, founders of Axonnic (
https://axonnic.com
). We’ve developed a forearm sleeve that reads muscle activity to decode finger movements and estimate fingertip force, while leaving the hands bare. It’s used to record human movement and generate training data for dextrous robots.
Here’s a demo video: https://youtube.com/shorts/xBrocTc9cfA
We’ve found that electromyography (EMG) is a much better way to train robots than by video alone because video only captures movement, not muscle activity or the effort behind the movement. A useful signal can be present even when the hand barely moves; just maintaining a grip involves muscle activation. The subtle muscle movements that can barely be picked up in video are the most important details for activities like sewing and delicate assembly.
The sleeve has 64 channels of surface electromyography, or EMG. Electrodes on the skin detect electrical activity from muscles in the forearm. We distribute sensors across the forearm so as to not overfit to one muscle group. We synchronize EMG with hand tracking to train a model that predicts finger joint angles, then we run the decoder solely from EMG, adding in fingertip force estimates that have been calibrated from finger presses on force sensors.
When the user takes the sleeve off then puts it back on again, the electrode positions change, so we run tests over separate wearings. In one case, we ran a 215-second recording, four days after training, without any recalibration, and compared the results with Apple Vision Pro hand tracking. The result was just 6.9° error across 20 joint angles. We’ve published the measurements and evaluation details here: https://axonnic.com/benchmarks.
We faced many challenges doing recordings in factories, including wireless interference and unreliable off-the-shelf hardware. This led to some bad recordings and the need to repeat data collection. For that reason, we’re developing our own electronics that use a wired PCB design that will eliminate interference and timing inconsistencies.
Axonnic grew out of Max's EMG research at Oxford. We looked at using the technology for computer control, then we thought a more promising use-case was in capturing the effort involved in skilled manual tasks. This technology could be described as a computer to human interface. Where computers gain insight and learn from human skills. Sewing particularly stood out because the material deforms and the operator is constantly adjusting grip and tension.
Maxim has an Oxford MBiol and conducted research on high-density surface EMG. He previously built internal tools at Skyscanner and worked at Voxblock across PCB development and supply chain. Arsh studied medicine at Oxford and has research experience applying machine learning to medical imaging, alongside software and robotics projects. Together we have built the sleeve, decoding software and data-collection system and tested them in industrial settings.
So far we have the tech being used to record sewing and other manual tasks at a European manufacturer, which signed an LOI for support with robotic implementation. We have also collected construction demonstrations involving electricians, plumbers and demolition work. These are pilot and data-collection examples. Separately, our public demos include controlling a Proception robotic hand from forearm EMG.
If you’ve done any of your own trials for training robots for manual tasks, we’d love to hear about what tasks you were trying to train for and how the trials went. We’re happy to discuss the hardware, calibration and models here in the comments. Thanks!
https://axonnic.com

articles.title: Show HN: Win98 PE Interpreter in WebAssembly – StarCraft and Diablo on Phones
articles.body:
Wine-Assembly: run real Windows 98 apps and games in your browser
Wine-Assembly is a Windows 98 emulator that runs the original, unmodified .exe files in a browser tab: 3D Pinball Space Cadet, SkiFree, Solitaire, FreeCell, Minesweeper, Notepad, Paint, Calculator, Winamp, the Windows Entertainment Pack, DirectDraw and Direct3D games, and 16-bit Windows 3.1 programs.
There is no operating-system image and no source port. An x86 interpreter and a reimplementation of the Win32 API are written directly in WebAssembly Text, and the guest program's machine code runs on them. Nothing is installed and nothing leaves your browser; a program's settings and scores stay in this browser's local storage.
Double-click an icon on the desktop to launch a program. On a phone, one tap opens it and games that need keys get on-screen controls.
- Every program on the desktop, with a page each: Pinball, Solitaire, Winamp, Paint, SkiFree and more
- How it works: articles on the x86 interpreter, lazy flags, real DLLs, software GDI, DirectX and Win16, plus the design docs and reverse-engineering notes
- How Wine-Assembly was built
- Source code on GitHub (MIT)

articles.title: Microsoft Outage Leads To Chlorine Gas Poisoning At German Theme Park
articles.body:
Microsoft Outage Leads To Chlorine Gas Poisoning At German Theme Park (www1.wdr.de) 50
			
		 	
				Slashdot readers djgl and Mirnotoriety shared a story about how a Microsoft Outlook outage contributed to a chlorine leak at Germany's Phantasialand theme park, injuring 15 guests, four of whom were hospitalized. German broadcasting institution WDR reports (translated to English):  We were all affected by this problem: On Friday, there was a disruption that crippled the US software company Microsoft, including its email program Outlook. Phantasialand was also affected. Due to the disruption, no emails were received, as the company informed WDR on Saturday. As a result, no one was aware that the sauna area's maintenance safety system had already issued an email alert. This was because the automatic dosing system had pumped too much chlorine into the pool.
Guests at the Hotel Ling Bao in Phantasialand, Bruhl, were injured as a result. They complained of health problems after visiting the pool. The pool was temporarily closed but has since been reopened, as the fire department informed WDR on Saturday. Due to complaints from hotel guests, emergency services and the fire department were called. Thirteen guests complained of respiratory irritation; ultimately, the number of affected individuals rose to a total of 15.  Cybersecurity architect and computer scientist Stephan Skrobisch said Microsoft is not responsible for the incident. "It's clearly the system's design that's the problem. They failed to implement an additional notification mechanism."
Slashdot reader davidwr agrees, writing in a comment: "Proper alarms would be a hardwired alarm that would be visible or audiable to someone who was on-site who could've gotten everyone out of the water. The blame for the injuries goes to the water park and/or whatever consultant told them it was okay not to have an on-site, hardwired alarm."

articles.title: Microsoft Blames Monster Email Outage On Software Defect Introduced In July Fix
articles.body:
Microsoft Blames Monster Email Outage On Software Defect Introduced In July Fix (theregister.com) 34
			
		 	
				Microsoft says last week's massive Microsoft 365 outage was caused by a software defect introduced in a July update that remained dormant until a Teams failover and a simultaneous 14% reduction in gateway capacity triggered a cascading failure. More than 80% of the affected gateway servers became unresponsive at the outage's worst point, and because the months-old change could not simply be rolled back, engineers spent roughly 15 hours developing and deploying a patch that restored the previous code path. The Register reports:  According to a preliminary post incident report published by Microsoft on November 15, the defect was introduced in July 2026. The update looked fine at the time, Microsoft says, having passed load testing and been deployed without any impact. However, the testing wasn't good enough. Microsoft's report states: "Our load testing tended to focus on weaker hardware with fewer cores." The defect caused "lock contention inside an internal Windows process which caused the machine's resources (CPU & memory) to be exhausted."
"The contention issue is worsened on machines with more cores and newer hardware." The fix containing the defect was prepared specifically for Microsoft 365 network gateway servers. Then two things happened at once. Teams failed over to the "primary" gateway that supports Exchange Online, creating a surge in load that was not, in itself, particularly unusual. At the same time, almost 14 percent of server capacity for the networking gateway was out of service, which wasn't a problem by itself either: it was on its way to being restored and, according to Microsoft, "the service had sufficient capacity headroom." Together, they pushed the gateway into the defect and chaos ensued. It was a classic cascading failure scenario. When a server loses connectivity, traffic gets routed to the next healthy endpoint. Which encountered the same problem. So traffic was rerouted again and... you can see where this was going. Within two hours, the defect was encountered across Microsoft's fleet. "At its lowest," the report states, "more than 80 percent of servers were unresponsive."
So, what to do? Bringing servers back to service didn't help -- they were immediately overwhelmed and fell over again. "Our normally automated recovery processes were not designed to restore service from this broad unresponsive state." A straightforward rollback was also not possible because the defect was months old. Instead, engineers developed patch for the patch or, in Microsoft's words, "an update that returned the code path to the previously known good state in Windows." The patch was applied to groups of servers and service was gradually restored.

articles.title: Optimizely compromised, served malware on Zoom, GitLab
articles.body:
On 16 November 2026, malicious JavaScript was served to visitors of 178 organisations through the Optimizely Web experimentation platform. The list includes some of the most visited sites in the world: Zoom, the BBC, CNN, Salesforce, GitLab, IKEA, HSBC, Equifax, Air France-KLM, Ledger and Peacock.
The malware was a multi-purpose kit. It swapped cryptocurrency wallet addresses for the attacker's, skimmed payment cards, stole cookies and screenshots, and on iPhones and iPads it delivered the Coruna and DarkSword iOS exploit kits. Crypto has already been stolen, with verified transactions to the attackers.
This is exactly the kind of attack Report URI is designed to detect. Our platform can identify unexpected changes to trusted JavaScript, detect new scripts being loaded and reveal suspicious connections to external destinations. In this case, those signals would have exposed the malicious activity, even though the original script was being served from a trusted Optimizely domain. With an appropriate CSP in enforcement mode, organisations could have gone a step further and blocked key parts of the attack before they succeeded.
The important lesson here is that trusted JavaScript doesn't always remain trustworthy. A website can be compromised through a third-party dependency without its own code or infrastructure ever being breached.
Most of the malicious code has now been removed. At 21:52 UTC we found it in only 1 of the 188 infected snippets, down from 169 at 20:56 UTC. If your site uses Optimizely Web, or you visited any of the sites below today, read on.
What happened
Optimizely Web works by having each customer load a JavaScript "snippet" from Optimizely's CDN, for example https://cdn.optimizely.com/js/6395285578973184.js. The snippet contains Optimizely's code, the customer's experiments and an optional field called Project JavaScript (projectJS): custom code the customer writes in their Optimizely dashboard, which runs on every page.
The attacker wrote their own code into the Project JavaScript of customer projects, and the rest of each snippet was untouched. The file was still served from cdn.optimizely.com, with Optimizely's certificate, from a host that every affected site already trusted. Here is what was added to Zoom's snippet:
A plain <script> tag pointing at https://1688360.cc/track.js (most snippets).
The same URL hidden in base64 with atob(). A search for "1688360.cc" won't find it. Smartsheet's snippet was cleaned at one point and then re-infected with this version, so whoever wrote the code still had access at the time.
A full inline copy of the payload, which runs through eval if 1688360.cc is blocked.
Some customers serve their snippet from their own domain, such as opt.scheels.com/js/<id>.js or www.vodafone.com.au/js/<id>.js. Those were affected too, because the content comes from the same Optimizely project.
We don't know how the attacker got write access to so many unrelated customer projects: a compromised Optimizely system, a compromised credential with cross-customer access, or something else. That's for Optimizely to explain. To be clear, Optimizely's CDN served exactly what it was given; this was not a CDN cache-poisoning attack. Optimizely's own sites were affected as well: the snippets for www.optimizely.com and login.optimizely.com both carried the code.
Timeline (UTC)
The payload was rebuilt 26 times during the day. The attacker added features, and added wallets but never removed any.
What the payload does
Every visitor received the same script, track.js, and every part of it was active at once. What a visitor experienced depended on their device and what they did on the page.
The script finds any valid wallet address (BTC, ETH and EVM chains, TRON, Solana, TON, Litecoin, Bitcoin Cash, Dogecoin) and replaces it with one of the attacker's. It validates checksums so it only swaps real addresses. It swaps them in:
page text, form fields, links and images;
the clipboard, on copy and through navigator.clipboard;
outgoing fetch/XHR requests, window.open, navigation and the iOS share sheet.
It re-scans the page whenever it changes. Copy an address from any affected page, or from anywhere else while that tab is open, and you may paste the attacker's.
2. Card skimming
Added at 13:43 UTC. The script watches form submissions and every fetch/XHR POST for a card number (Luhn-checked), expiry date and CVV. When it has all three, it sends them to https://1688360.cc/card.php with navigator.sendBeacon. Cards entered in hosted payment iframes (Stripe, Adyen and similar) were out of its reach. Cards typed into a site's own form fields were not.
3. Cookie and screenshot theft
When it swaps an address next to wallet or payment wording, it sends the following to https://1688360.cc/hit.php:
the page URL;
document.cookie (cookies not marked HttpOnly);
the original addresses it replaced;
a screenshot of the page, rendered with html2canvas.
4. iOS exploit kits: Coruna and DarkSword
On iPhones and iPads the script loads boot.js from 5vobauua3ojpklx.icu and eil786npto9u5bq.icu. It reads the iOS version and loads an exploit chain in a hidden iframe:
The Coruna loader is byte-identical to a sample we analysed in October from a different campaign. The kit's own comments say iOS 18.7.3 and later, and 26.3 and later, are patched. Pages on iOS 18.6 or earlier reload every 60 seconds to retry the exploit, which is a visible symptom.
Money stolen so far
As of 19:25 UTC on 16 November, the attacker's wallets had received about $7,040, all within roughly nine hours on the 16th:
Funds were swept out at 13:03 to 13:05 UTC. The USDC on Ethereum went to a HitBTC deposit address. The TRON wallet has been in use since March 2026, so this actor was active long before this campaign. We cannot see how many cards or cookies reached 1688360.cc.
Who was affected
We fetched 1,611 distinct Optimizely snippets, found mostly through our own crawl data, and checked each one for the malicious code. 188 snippets belonging to 178 organisations were infected. We kept a copy of every infected file, along with its response headers, SHA-256 hash and fetch time as evidence. The real number is likely higher as we could only check snippets we could find in time.
By sector
Full list
Ranked by Tranco position within each sector and the status at 21:52 UTC: every snippet except TalkTalk's had been cleaned.
Banking & Finance (32)
Technology & SaaS (23)
Retail & Fashion (20)
Streaming & Entertainment (12)
News & Media (10)
Airlines & Travel (9)
Healthcare & Pharma (8)
Industrial & Manufacturing (8)
Telecoms (7)
Crypto & Trading (6)
Insurance (6)
Property & Real Estate (6)
Food & Hospitality (5)
Home & Smart Home (5)
Nonprofit & Civic (4)
Gambling (4)
Professional Services (4)
Logistics & Shipping (3)
Automotive (3)
Education (3)
The earlier webshell.lol wave, through Kissmetrics, StorifyMe and Minute Media, affected other sites and isn't included above.
How Report URI would have detected, or even prevented, this attack
Every one of these needs only a CSP in Report-Only mode, so nothing on the site breaks:
It's possible to go even further and deploy a CSP that could actively block these attacks and prevent any data breach happening. The websites affected by this attack weren't necessarily running vulnerable code of their own, they were loading JavaScript from a provider they trusted, and that trust was exploited. This is why monitoring what runs in your visitors' browsers is so important. Report URI gives organisations the visibility to detect when trusted dependencies change or behave unexpectedly, and the tools to help enforce policies that prevent malicious scripts and connections from succeeding.
Did Content Security Policy help?
We crawled 256 of the affected organisations' own hosts and evaluated their CSP against what this payload needs:
Load track.js from 1688360.cc.
Or run the inline fallback, which needs 'unsafe-eval' or 'unsafe-inline'.
Send stolen data to 1688360.cc (connect-src).
Load the iOS kit (script-src, frame-src).
Allowing cdn.optimizely.com was never going to help. The malicious code arrived from the trusted host itself. What separated the 24 protected sites from the rest was a restrictive script-src. A site that lists only the hosts it needs blocks 1688360.cc. Two common settings let it straight through:
'strict-dynamic': any script the trusted Optimizely snippet inserts is trusted too.
'unsafe-eval', which Optimizely's own documentation tells customers to allow: the inline-fallback version ran through eval even where track.js was blocked. That is what happened at HSBC. Its CSP blocked track.js and the data theft, but the inline copy still ran.
connect-src matters. The 17 "partial" sites blocked card, cookie and screenshot theft because they restrict where the page can send data. That doesn't stop address swapping, which happens inside the page.
What to do now
If your site uses Optimizely Web:
Open every project's Project JavaScript and every experiment's custom code. Look for 1688360.cc, atob( and any script you didn't write.
Review who and what has write access to your Optimizely account (users, API tokens, integrations) and rotate credentials.
If you have card fields in your own forms, treat cards entered on 16 November as potentially exposed.
Treat any session tokens or secrets in non-HttpOnly cookies as exposed, and rotate them.
Deploy a CSP. Restrict connect-src, avoid 'unsafe-eval' where you can, and turn on reporting.
Consider if you need to communicate to your customers about having served them malware.
If you visited an affected site on 16 November:
Update your iPhone or iPad to iOS 18.7.3 or later, or iOS 26.3 or later.
Check any crypto transfer you made. If the address you pasted doesn't match the one you meant to pay, it may have been swapped.
Watch your card statements if you paid by card on an affected site.
Indicators of compromise
All of these domains are attacker-owned; block them including subdomains.
Attacker wallets: BTC 19g9rZcPeiz8rUvyWpTRyXXhPnjsWrc3kW ETH/EVM 0xC4026b06D82b0F0B363eda0642D61CfbDc17884e TRON THvs6p56XkUiMkJeSc51cAP64u2RsTYqxa SOL FVtL8NMYS9PA1v3HE67XUGCtGA9JaZUvqav2fU2LrV5n TON UQAgM1VqSZQiJLSG5w-ovurq5CZdxLEK3_7CMmwALTA5e09p LTC ltc1q3wp7g6ds0ggg6fl6kncpa4sepn0q3qfacgred5 BCH qzkaaf8n6grmpr0d9lx8xutn3r9lk722f566hhpe58 DOGE DBEGrxRF7KMSuhTS4c1MFviStU6efdMnu5
We keep an archive of every infected snippet with hashes and timestamps, and can share it with affected organisations and CERTs on request. During research and investigation, once we were confident that Optimizely was the source, we began efforts to reach out via various channels and provide the full details. At the time of publication, we have not had any response.
